3.s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I (Date/Event)
a. 21 March
b. 21 June
c. 23 September
d. 22 December
List-II (Sun overhead)
i. Tropic of Capricorn
ii. Equator
iii. Tropic of Cancer
iv. Equator

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
3.x: On 21 March the Sun is overhead at the Equator; on 21 June at the Tropic of Cancer; on 23 September at the Equator; and on 22 December at the Tropic of Capricorn.
3.tq: Start from the solstice pair and then place the two equinoxes at the Equator.
3.sec: Revolution effects - solstices, equinoxes, seasons, day length  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

3.s: On 21 June, which one of the following conditions is associated with the Northern Hemisphere?
o: Sun overhead at the Tropic of Capricorn
3.x: 21 June is the Northern Hemisphere’s summer solstice. The Sun is overhead at the Tropic of Cancer, producing the longest day and summer conditions there.
3.tq: Link the date, overhead latitude and seasonal effect in the relevant hemisphere.
3.sec: Revolution effects - solstices, equinoxes, seasons, day length  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

3.s: Which of the following dates is associated with the winter solstice in the Northern Hemisphere?
3.x: The Northern Hemisphere experiences its winter solstice on 22 December, when the Sun is overhead at the Tropic of Capricorn.
3.tq: Use the solstice-equinox calendar sequence to identify the winter date.
3.sec: Revolution effects - solstices, equinoxes, seasons, day length  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

3.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. During the equinoxes, day and night are approximately equal everywhere.
2. The equator experiences approximately 12-hour days throughout the year.
3. The poles experience six months of daylight and six months of darkness.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
3.x: The equinoxes bring approximately equal day and night worldwide. The equator has nearly 12-hour days throughout the year, while the poles experience roughly six months of day and six months of night.
3.tq: Combine three day-length facts across different latitudes and seasons.
3.sec: Revolution effects - solstices, equinoxes, seasons, day length  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

3.s: The seasons on Earth are primarily caused by
o: the tilt of Earth’s axis together with its revolution around the Sun
the elliptical shape of the Moon’s orbit
the changing distance between Earth and the Moon
the daily rotation of Earth alone
3.x: Seasons result mainly from the tilt of Earth’s axis combined with Earth’s revolution around the Sun, which changes the angle and duration of solar illumination.
3.tq: Identify the combined cause rather than selecting a single-motion explanation.
3.sec: Revolution effects - solstices, equinoxes, seasons, day length  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

3.s: During the summer season in the Southern Hemisphere, which pole is tilted towards the Sun?
3.x: During southern summer, the South Pole is tilted towards the Sun, producing longer days and summer conditions in the Southern Hemisphere.
3.tq: Relate the hemisphere experiencing summer to the direction of axial tilt.
3.sec: Revolution effects - solstices, equinoxes, seasons, day length  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

3.s:
Arrange the following events in chronological order within a year:
A. Winter solstice
B. Vernal equinox
C. Summer solstice
D. Autumnal equinox
3.x: The sequence is vernal equinox around 21 March, summer solstice around 21 June, autumnal equinox around 22/23 September, and winter solstice around 22 December.
3.tq: Fix the sequence using the four annual astronomical markers.
3.sec: Revolution effects - solstices, equinoxes, seasons, day length  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

3.s: In which direction does the Earth rotate when viewed from above the North Pole?
3.x: The Earth rotates from west to east. This appears anticlockwise when viewed from above the North Pole, producing the apparent eastward movement of the Sun.
3.tq: Use the viewpoint carefully and distinguish the actual rotation from the apparent movement of the Sun.
3.sec: Rotation - direction, speed, circle of illumination, effects

3.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Earth—west to east; Venus and Uranus—opposite direction
Earth, Venus and Uranus—all rotate west to east
Earth—east to west; Venus and Uranus—west to east
Earth and Venus—east to west; Uranus—west to east
3.x: Earth rotates west to east, whereas Venus and Uranus spin in the opposite direction.
3.tq: Discriminate between the rotational directions of Earth and the two exceptional planets.
3.sec: Rotation - direction, speed, circle of illumination, effects

3.s: The time taken by the Earth to complete one rotation with reference to the distant stars is approximately
3.x: The Earth takes about 23 hours 56 minutes to complete a sidereal rotation. The ordinary solar day is approximately 24 hours.
3.tq: Distinguish the sidereal day from the solar day when two close time values are given.
3.sec: Rotation - direction, speed, circle of illumination, effects

3.s: The circle of illumination is best described as the line that
o: marks the boundary between the tropics and polar regions
divides the illuminated half of the Earth from the dark half
joins all places having the same local time
divides the Earth into the Eastern and Western Hemispheres
3.x: The circle of illumination, or terminator, separates the day side of the Earth from its night side.
3.tq: Match the geographical term with its precise definition rather than with a related latitude concept.
3.sec: Rotation - direction, speed, circle of illumination, effects

3.s: The circle of illumination passes through both the North and South Poles only during the
3.x: At the equinoxes, the circle of illumination passes through both poles and day and night are nearly equal across the Earth.
3.tq: Use the seasonal event associated with equal illumination of the two hemispheres.
3.sec: Rotation - direction, speed, circle of illumination, effects

3.s:
With reference to the effects of the Earth's rotation, consider the following statements:
1. The Coriolis force deflects moving winds and currents to the right in the Northern Hemisphere.
2. The Coriolis force deflects moving winds and currents to the left in the Southern Hemisphere.
3. Rotation contributes to the flattening of the Earth at the poles.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
3.x: All three statements are correct. Rotation produces opposite Coriolis deflections in the two hemispheres and contributes to polar flattening.
3.tq: Combine the directional effect of Coriolis force with the physical effect of rotation.
3.sec: Rotation - direction, speed, circle of illumination, effects

3.s: According to the cited 2026 observation, melting ice can lengthen the day because it
o: increases the Earth's distance from the Sun
stops the movement of the tectonic plates
moves mass towards the Equator and increases the length of rotation
moves mass away from the Equator and slows the rotation
3.x: Melting ice redistributes mass towards the Equator, slowing the Earth's rotation and lengthening the day by about 1.33 milliseconds per century.
3.tq: Trace the stated cause-effect chain instead of treating climate change as an unrelated process.
3.sec: Rotation - direction, speed, circle of illumination, effects

3.s: The Equator crosses which one of the following groups of countries?
o: India, Bangladesh, Myanmar and Saudi Arabia
3.x: The Equator crosses Ecuador, Colombia, Brazil and Kenya. The other groups contain countries associated mainly with the Tropic of Cancer or Tropic of Capricorn.
3.tq: Identify the latitude by matching it with a distinctive group of countries.
3.sec: Equator and other key latitudes - countries crossed, number of parallels and meridians

3.s: Which one of the following countries is NOT crossed by the Equator?
3.x: The Equator crosses Gabon, Uganda and Somalia, but it does not touch India. India's nearest point to the Equator is Indira Point at 6°45' N.
3.tq: Find the country outside the listed Equatorial belt and use the India-specific exception.
3.sec: Equator and other key latitudes - countries crossed, number of parallels and meridians

3.s: Which one of the following countries is associated with the Tropic of Cancer?
3.x: The Tropic of Cancer at 23°26' N crosses Saudi Arabia. Madagascar, Namibia and Mozambique are associated with the Tropic of Capricorn.
3.tq: Separate the northern Tropic of Cancer from the southern Tropic of Capricorn using the country location.
3.sec: Equator and other key latitudes - countries crossed, number of parallels and meridians

3.s: Which one of the following sequences contains only countries crossed by the Tropic of Capricorn?
o: China, Myanmar, Saudi Arabia and India
3.x: The Tropic of Capricorn at 23°26' S crosses Chile, Argentina, Paraguay and Brazil. The remaining groups contain countries crossed by the Equator or Tropic of Cancer.
3.tq: Use latitude signs and hemispheric location to eliminate mixed country groups.
3.sec: Equator and other key latitudes - countries crossed, number of parallels and meridians

3.s: The Arctic Circle and Antarctic Circle are located approximately at
3.x: The Arctic Circle lies at approximately 66°33' N and the Antarctic Circle at approximately 66°33' S. They mark the approximate limits of polar day and polar night.
3.tq: Match the paired northern and southern latitudes with their corresponding circles.
3.sec: Equator and other key latitudes - countries crossed, number of parallels and meridians

3.s: How many parallels of latitude and meridians of longitude are conventionally drawn on the globe?
3.x: There are 90 parallels north of the Equator, 90 south of it and the Equator itself, making 181 parallels. There are 360 meridians of longitude.
3.tq: Break the latitude count into 90 north, 90 south and the Equator before selecting the pair.
3.sec: Equator and other key latitudes - countries crossed, number of parallels and meridians

3.s: One degree of latitude is approximately equal to
3.x: One degree of latitude corresponds to approximately 111 kilometres on the Earth's surface.
3.tq: Distinguish the standard one-degree latitude distance from its decimal and unit traps.
3.sec: Equator and other key latitudes - countries crossed, number of parallels and meridians

3.s: Which one of the following statements about the Equator and India is correct?
o: The Equator passes through Indira Point.
The Equator passes through the central part of the Indian mainland.
The Equator passes through southern India.
The Equator does not touch India, and Indira Point is India's nearest point to it.
3.x: The Equator does not touch India. Indira Point, at 6°45' N, is India's nearest point to the Equator.
3.tq: Use the precise exception rather than assuming that the southernmost Indian point lies on the Equator.
3.sec: Equator and other key latitudes - countries crossed, number of parallels and meridians

3.s: The Earth's axis is inclined to the perpendicular to the plane of its orbit by approximately
3.x: The Earth's axis is tilted 23½° from the perpendicular to the orbital plane. Consequently, it makes an angle of 66½° with the orbital plane itself.
3.tq: Read the reference line carefully: inclination to the perpendicular is different from inclination to the orbital plane.
3.sec: Axial tilt and inclination - consequences, observed shift

3.s: The angle made by the Earth's axis with the plane of its orbit is approximately
3.x: The Earth's axis makes an angle of 66½° with the plane of its orbit, equivalent to a tilt of 23½° from the perpendicular.
3.tq: Discriminate between the two complementary angles associated with axial inclination.
3.sec: Axial tilt and inclination - consequences, observed shift

3.s:
Which of the following are consequences of the Earth's axial tilt?
1. Formation of seasons
2. Unequal length of day and night
3. Location of the tropics at approximately 23½°
4. Location of the polar circles at approximately 66½°
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
3.x: Axial tilt is responsible for seasons and unequal day length, and it determines the positions of both the tropics and polar circles.
3.tq: Treat the tropics and polar circles as geometric consequences of the same axial tilt.
3.sec: Axial tilt and inclination - consequences, observed shift

3.s: Which one of the following statements regarding axial precession is correct?
o: Precession changes the number of meridians drawn on the globe.
The pole star remains permanently fixed because the axis does not move.
Vega is located on the Equator and determines the seasons every year.
The celestial pole pointed to Vega about 14,000 years ago and is expected to point there again in about 12,000 years.
3.x: The Earth's axis slowly wobbles, changing the direction of the celestial pole. Vega was the pole star approximately 14,000 years ago and is expected to assume that role again in about 12,000 years.
3.tq: Use the time-scale and the named star to identify the correct precession statement.
3.sec: Axial tilt and inclination - consequences, observed shift

3.s: The long-term orbital and axial variations that influence climate are collectively known as
3.x: Long-period variations in Earth's orbit and axial behaviour that influence climate are called Milankovitch cycles.
3.tq: Match the named climate mechanism with orbital and axial variations rather than atmospheric circulation.
3.sec: Axial tilt and inclination - consequences, observed shift

3.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched with the extreme points of India?
3.x: Indira Col in the Karakoram is India's northernmost point, while Guhar Moti in Gujarat is its westernmost point.
3.tq: Start with the sure extreme-point pair and reject options that interchange directional extremes.
3.sec: Latitude and longitude extent of India and AP

3.s: Which one of the following correctly states the approximate north-south and east-west dimensions of India?
3.x: India extends approximately 3,214 km from north to south and 2,933 km from east to west.
3.tq: Do not reverse the directional dimensions when two close figures are presented.
3.sec: Latitude and longitude extent of India and AP

3.s: Which one of the following statements about India's geographical position is correct?
o: India lies entirely in the Northern Hemisphere and has a land frontier of about 15,200 km.
India lies entirely in the Western Hemisphere and has a 9,740 km land frontier.
India lies in both hemispheres and has no land frontier.
India lies entirely in the Southern Hemisphere.
3.x: India lies entirely in the Northern Hemisphere and its land frontier is approximately 15,200 km.
3.tq: Check the hemisphere and the approximate frontier figure together to avoid a location trap.
3.sec: Latitude and longitude extent of India and AP

3.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Southernmost mainland point—Indira Point; easternmost point—Guhar Moti
Easternmost point—Indira Col; westernmost point—Indira Point
3.x: Kanyakumari is the southernmost point of mainland India and Kibithu in Arunachal Pradesh is the easternmost point of India.
3.tq: Match each extreme with its directional label and reject swapped east-west or mainland-island pairs.
3.sec: Latitude and longitude extent of India and AP

3.s: Which one of the following statements regarding Andhra Pradesh is correct?
o: It extends approximately from 8°4' N to 37°6' N and from 68°7' E to 97°25' E.
It extends approximately from 23°26' N to 66°33' N and from 82°30' E to 97°25' E.
It extends approximately from 12°41' N to 19°07' N and from 77° E to 84°40' E.
It extends approximately from 12°41' S to 19°07' S and from 77° W to 84°40' W.
3.x: Andhra Pradesh extends approximately from 12°41' N to 19°07' N latitude and 77° E to 84°40' E longitude.
3.tq: Separate the state extent from the much larger national extent and check the hemisphere symbols.
3.sec: Latitude and longitude extent of India and AP

3.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Andhra Pradesh:
1. Its area is approximately 1,62,970 square kilometres.
2. It accounts for approximately 4.96 per cent of India's area.
3. It is described as the seventh largest state.
4. Its coastline is approximately 974 km long.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
3.x: All four statements are correct: Andhra Pradesh has an area of about 1,62,970 sq km, around 4.96% of India's area, is the seventh largest state and has a coastline of about 974 km.
3.tq: Check each numerical statement independently before choosing the combined code.
3.sec: Latitude and longitude extent of India and AP

3.s: Andhra Pradesh is one of the how many Indian States through which the Indian Standard Time meridian passes?
3.x: The IST meridian at 82.5° E passes through five Indian States, including Andhra Pradesh.
3.tq: Treat the state count as a direct numerical fact and avoid substituting the number of states crossed by another latitude.
3.sec: Universal angles

3.s: The IST Rules, 2026 were notified on
3.x: The IST Rules, 2026 were notified on 27 August 2026. The dates in June, July and August 31 refer to other cited developments or reports.
3.tq: Separate the notification date from the dates of associated reports and network developments.
3.sec: Universal angles

3.s: The White Rabbit IST network is significant primarily because it supports
o: the measurement of the Earth's circumference by satellite imagery
synchronised high-precision time-stamps for critical infrastructure and helps protect against GPS spoofing
the replacement of the IST meridian by local solar time
the drawing of new parallels and meridians on the globe
3.x: The White Rabbit IST network enables synchronised IST time-stamps for banking, digital payments, railways, airports, power grids and telecom, and helps protect against GPS spoofing.
3.tq: Link the technology with its stated operational uses and security function.
3.sec: Universal angles

3.s:
Consider the following statements regarding India's single-time-zone debate:
1. A single time zone in a country about two hours wide can cost the north-eastern region daylight hours.
2. Proposals for separate time zones have been finally implemented.
3. The proposals for separate time zones remain undecided.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
3.x: Statement 1 is correct because the wide east-west extent creates a daylight disadvantage in the north-east. Statement 2 is false: separate-zone proposals remain undecided, making statement 3 correct.
3.tq: Find the false statement by checking whether the proposal is implemented or still under debate.
3.sec: Universal angles

3.s: Which one of the following is NOT listed as a significance of synchronised IST time-stamps?
o: Determining the chemical composition of rocks
3.x: Synchronised IST time-stamps are significant for banking, digital payments, railways, airports, power grids and telecommunications. Determining rock composition is unrelated to this function.
3.tq: Identify the unrelated application among several infrastructure and communication uses.
3.sec: Universal angles

4.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
4.x: At the winter solstice, the Sun is overhead at the Tropic of Capricorn. The equinoxes have the Sun overhead at the Equator, while the summer solstice occurs over the Tropic of Cancer.
4.tq: Start from the sure pair and eliminate the reversed overhead-Sun locations.
4.sec: Solstices and equinoxes → dates and overhead Sun  [APPSC]

4.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The autumnal equinox in the Northern Hemisphere occurs around 22 or 23 September.
2. The winter solstice in the Northern Hemisphere occurs around 22 December.
3. The summer solstice occurs when the Sun is overhead at the Tropic of Capricorn.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
4.x: The autumnal equinox occurs around 22 or 23 September and the winter solstice around 22 December. The summer solstice has the overhead Sun at the Tropic of Cancer, not Capricorn.
4.tq: Use the incorrect overhead-Sun statement to split the coded options.
4.sec: Solstices and equinoxes → dates and overhead Sun  [APPSC]

4.s: The International Day of Yoga is observed on which date, which also corresponds to the summer solstice in the Northern Hemisphere?
4.x: The International Day of Yoga is observed on 21 June, the date of the Northern Hemisphere’s summer solstice.
4.tq: Use the date-event association rather than confusing it with an equinox date.
4.sec: Solstices and equinoxes → dates and overhead Sun  [APPSC]

4.s: Which combination most accurately explains the seasonal variation in the angle of incidence of solar rays and the length of day?
o: Rotation alone and changing distance from the Sun
Ocean currents, tides and the changing speed of winds
Axial inclination, parallelism of the axis, revolution and the spherical shape of the Earth
The elliptical orbit alone and the rotation of the Moon
4.x: Seasonal variation results from the Earth’s axial inclination, the parallelism of its axis, its revolution around the Sun and its spherical shape. These alter the Sun’s angle and the duration of daylight received by different regions.
4.tq: Identify the complete causal combination instead of accepting the distance-from-Sun misconception.
4.sec: Causes of seasons and day-length variation  [APPSC]

4.s:
Assertion (A): When the Northern Hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun, it experiences summer.
Reason (R): The hemisphere tilted towards the Sun receives more direct rays and has longer days.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
4.x: Both statements are true. A hemisphere tilted towards the Sun receives more direct insolation and longer daylight, producing summer conditions.
4.tq: Check whether the reason directly explains the seasonal condition.
4.sec: Causes of seasons and day-length variation  [APPSC]

4.s: Which one of the following statements is correct regarding the parallelism of the Earth’s axis?
o: The axis points towards the Sun during the Northern Hemisphere summer.
The axis is perpendicular to the orbital plane throughout the year.
The axis generally maintains its parallelism and points towards the Pole Star.
The axis changes its direction completely during every revolution.
4.x: The Earth’s axis maintains its parallelism during revolution and generally points towards the Pole Star. This contributes to the seasonal change in the distribution of sunlight.
4.tq: Test the exact meaning of a commonly confused astronomical term.
4.sec: Causes of seasons and day-length variation  [APPSC]

4.s: Which latitude zone experiences the greatest seasonal differences in day length and insolation?
4.x: Seasonal differences are greatest in high latitudes because the annual swings in day length and insolation are very large there.
4.tq: Use the latitude-based comparison and avoid reversing the trend.
4.sec: Seasonal contrast by latitude zone  [APPSC]

4.s:
Consider the following statements regarding seasons in different latitude zones:
1. Low-latitude regions generally have small annual temperature contrasts.
2. In low latitudes, seasons are often marked by wet and dry periods.
3. Mid-latitude regions generally experience four distinct seasons.
4. Subtropical regions have hot summers and mild winters.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
4.x: All four statements are correct. Low latitudes commonly have wet and dry seasons, subtropical regions have hot summers and mild winters, and mid-latitudes show four distinct seasons.
4.tq: When every statement expresses a stated latitude-zone characteristic, select the complete combination.
4.sec: Seasonal contrast by latitude zone  [APPSC]

4.s: At the Equator, the approximate duration of daylight on 21 June, on an equinox, and on 22 December is respectively:
4.x: At the Equator, day and night are approximately equal throughout the year, with about 12 hours of daylight on these dates.
4.tq: Use the equatorial invariance to eliminate solstice-based extremes.
4.sec: Day length on solstices and equinoxes at different latitudes  [APPSC]

4.s: Which one of the following correctly represents the approximate daylight duration at the Tropic of Cancer on 21 June and 22 December?
4.x: At the Tropic of Cancer, daylight lasts approximately 13½ hours on 21 June and 10½ hours on 22 December.
4.tq: Compare the two solstices by identifying the longer day in the tilted hemisphere.
4.sec: Day length on solstices and equinoxes at different latitudes  [APPSC]

4.s: On 21 June, which one of the following pairs correctly describes the condition at the Arctic Circle and the North Pole?
o: Arctic Circle—24-hour night; North Pole—continuous night
Arctic Circle—continuous day; North Pole—24-hour night
Arctic Circle—12-hour day; North Pole—sunrise and sunset
Arctic Circle—24-hour day; North Pole—continuous day
4.x: On 21 June, the Arctic Circle experiences a 24-hour day, while the North Pole is in continuous daylight.
4.tq: Separate the polar-circle condition from the polar-point condition.
4.sec: Day length on solstices and equinoxes at different latitudes  [APPSC]

4.s: At the North Pole, which sequence correctly describes the conditions on 21 June, around an equinox, and on 22 December?
o: Continuous night, sunrise and sunset, continuous day
Continuous day, sunrise and sunset, continuous night
Sunrise and sunset, continuous night, continuous day
4.x: The North Pole has continuous daylight around the June solstice, sunrise or sunset at an equinox, and continuous night around the December solstice.
4.tq: Track the annual polar light sequence from June through December.
4.sec: Day length on solstices and equinoxes at different latitudes  [APPSC]

4.s: Which one of the following statements correctly compares the solstices of the two hemispheres?
o: The Northern Hemisphere has its longest day around 22 December, whereas the Southern Hemisphere has it on 21 June.
The Northern Hemisphere has its longest day on 21 June, whereas the Southern Hemisphere has its longest day around 22 December.
The longest day occurs in both hemispheres on 21 June.
Both hemispheres have their shortest day on 21 June.
4.x: The Northern Hemisphere has its longest day around 21 June, while the Southern Hemisphere has its longest day around 22 December. Their seasonal cycles are opposite.
4.tq: Use the reversed seasonal relationship between the two hemispheres.
4.sec: Seasons in northern vs southern hemisphere  [other exams]

4.s: Christmas in Australia generally falls during which season?
4.x: Australia lies in the Southern Hemisphere, where December corresponds to summer.
4.tq: Apply the hemisphere-season reversal to a familiar calendar event.
4.sec: Seasons in northern vs southern hemisphere  [other exams]

4.s: Which one of the following places does NOT receive the overhead Sun at noon on any day of the year?
4.x: Only places between the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn can receive the overhead Sun. Delhi, being north of 23½°N, never does so.
4.tq: Apply the tropical-latitude boundary to identify the exception.
4.sec: Noon shadow length and June day length at Indian cities  [other exams]

4.s: On 21 June, where is the noon shadow absent because the Sun is overhead?
4.x: On 21 June, the Sun is overhead at the Tropic of Cancer, so an object there casts no shadow at local noon.
4.tq: Link the solstice date with the corresponding overhead latitude.
4.sec: Noon shadow length and June day length at Indian cities  [other exams]

4.s: Which of the following correctly represents the order of June day length from greatest to least among the listed Indian cities?
4.x: On 21 June, day length increases northward. Therefore, the order is Srinagar, Delhi, Hyderabad, Chennai and Kanyakumari.
4.tq: Arrange locations by latitude before comparing their June daylight.
4.sec: Noon shadow length and June day length at Indian cities  [other exams]

4.s: Which one of the following statements regarding Andhra Pradesh is correct?
o: Andhra Pradesh lies between the Equator and the Tropic of Cancer and can receive the overhead Sun twice a year.
Andhra Pradesh lies between the Tropic of Capricorn and the Equator and never receives the overhead Sun.
Andhra Pradesh lies entirely north of the Tropic of Cancer.
Andhra Pradesh experiences continuous daylight in June.
4.x: Andhra Pradesh extends approximately from 12°41′N to 19°07′N, between the Equator and the Tropic of Cancer. Hence, the overhead Sun can occur there twice a year.
4.tq: Use the state’s latitude range to infer its solar position and temperature conditions.
4.sec: Noon shadow length and June day length at Indian cities  [other exams]

4.s: Which of the following is NOT a factor affecting the distribution of insolation?
o: Angle of incidence of solar rays
4.x: The major factors listed are the angle of incidence, duration of day, atmospheric transparency and land configuration. Direction of ocean tides is not one of them.
4.tq: Find the unrelated factor among the components of insolation distribution.
4.sec: Insolation distribution - angle, day length, latitude

4.s: Why do vertical solar rays generally produce greater heating than oblique rays?
o: They occur only during the winter season.
They are reflected completely by the atmosphere.
They concentrate the received energy over a smaller surface area and generally pass through less atmosphere.
They travel through a greater thickness of atmosphere and heat a smaller area.
4.x: Vertical rays are more concentrated over a smaller area and usually pass through a shorter atmospheric path, producing stronger heating than oblique rays.
4.tq: Connect the angle of incidence with both concentration and atmospheric passage.
4.sec: Insolation distribution - angle, day length, latitude

4.s: Which one of the following statements about the global distribution of insolation is correct?
o: The maximum insolation is always received at the Equator because it is closest to the Sun.
The poles receive maximum insolation because of their long summer days alone.
Insolation increases steadily from the tropics towards the poles.
Insolation generally decreases from the tropics towards the poles, while subtropical deserts may receive maximum insolation because of cloudless skies.
4.x: Insolation generally decreases from the tropics to the poles. Subtropical deserts can receive the maximum because their cloudless skies permit intense solar heating; the Equator is not necessarily the maximum zone.
4.tq: Separate the general latitudinal trend from the subtropical-desert maximum.
4.sec: Insolation distribution - angle, day length, latitude

4.s: The hot weather season in India associated with the northward march of the Sun generally extends from:
4.x: The northward march of the Sun is associated with India’s hot weather season from March to May.
4.tq: Match the seasonal period with the associated apparent movement of the Sun.
4.sec: Insolation distribution - angle, day length, latitude

4.s: Which one of the following statements regarding India’s pre-monsoon conditions is correct?
o: Pre-monsoon rainfall is absent from peninsular India.
Pre-monsoon showers occur exclusively in the Himalayan region.
About two-thirds of annual rainfall occurs during the pre-monsoon season only.
About 10% of the annual rainfall occurs as pre-monsoon rain, including coffee-blossom showers in South India.
4.x: Approximately 10% of India’s annual rainfall occurs during the pre-monsoon period. Coffee-blossom showers are associated particularly with South India.
4.tq: Use the rainfall percentage and the regional example to reject exaggerated claims.

Movement of granite in the mantle
5.x: The churning motion of molten iron in the liquid outer core drives the geodynamo, which generates Earth's magnetic field.
5.tq: Match the process with its physical location and consequence.
5.sec: Core - outer vs inner core, constituents besides iron and nickel  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

5.s: Which one of the following statements regarding the inner core is correct?
o: It is solid and has a density of approximately 13.3–13.6 g/cm³.
It is liquid and has a density of about 4.6 g/cm³.
It is plastic and lies above the Moho.
It is gaseous and lies between 100 and 200 km depth.
5.x: The inner core is solid, extends from approximately 5,150 to 6,371 km depth and has a density of about 13.3–13.6 g/cm³.
5.tq: Reject the state-depth reversals and select the precise inner-core description.
5.sec: Core - outer vs inner core, constituents besides iron and nickel  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

5.s: P-waves cross the inner core at approximately what velocity?
5.x: P-waves cross the inner core at approximately 11.23 km/s.
5.tq: Distinguish the seismic velocity figure from density and average-Earth values.
5.sec: Core - outer vs inner core, constituents besides iron and nickel  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

5.s: In the terminology used by Suess, NIFE refers primarily to:
5.x: NIFE denotes the iron-nickel composition associated with the Earth's core.
5.tq: Discriminate among SIAL, SIMA and NIFE by their compositional meanings.
5.sec: Core - outer vs inner core, constituents besides iron and nickel  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

5.s: Which one of the following statements about the recent observations of the outer core is correct?
o: The solid inner core stopped rotating in 2020.
The outer core became completely solid beneath the Pacific after 2020.
The liquid outer core beneath the Pacific changed from strong eastward flow to sluggish westward flow after 2020.
The liquid outer core beneath the Pacific changed from sluggish westward flow to strong eastward flow, with weakening around 2020.
5.x: Swarm satellite observations indicated a shift beneath the Pacific from sluggish westward flow to strong eastward flow, followed by weakening around 2020.
5.tq: Watch for the reversed-direction trap in a dynamic current-affairs statement.
5.sec: Core - outer vs inner core, constituents besides iron and nickel  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

5.s: Which one of the following statements about mantle earthquakes is correct?
o: They occur only within the continental crust.
They occur only at the Earth's surface and produce the strongest surface shaking.
They are confined to the liquid outer core.
They occur more than 80 km below the Moho and generally produce weak surface shaking.
5.x: The global mapping referred to mantle earthquakes occurring more than 80 km below the Moho; their surface shaking is generally weak.
5.tq: Use the depth and surface-effect combination to identify the correct statement.
5.sec: Universal angles

5.s: Diamonds reach the Earth's crust from the mantle mainly through:
5.x: Diamonds formed in the mantle are transported upward to the crust through kimberlite pipes.
5.tq: Match the resource with its geological transport pathway.
5.sec: Universal angles

5.s: Which State is associated with approximately 90% of India's diamond reserves?
5.x: Madhya Pradesh is associated with approximately 90% of India's diamond reserves.
5.tq: Link the percentage resource fact with the correct State rather than a geothermal location.
5.sec: Universal angles

5.s: The liquid outer core is significant for life on Earth because the magnetic field generated by it:
o: Prevents the formation of continental crust.
Shields life from solar wind and cosmic radiation.
5.x: The magnetic field generated by the liquid outer core helps shield life from the solar wind and cosmic radiation.
5.tq: Apply the geodynamo-magnetic-field relationship to its environmental significance.
5.sec: Universal angles

5.s: Magnetic reversals of the Earth may last for periods of up to approximately:
5.x: The duration of magnetic reversals has been reported to extend up to approximately 70,000 years.
5.tq: Distinguish the order of magnitude among closely spaced numerical options.
5.sec: Universal angles

6.s: Which element constitutes the highest percentage by weight of the Earth's crust?
6.x: Oxygen is the most abundant element in the Earth's crust, constituting approximately 46.6% by weight.
6.tq: Use the direct-ranking approach for numerical abundance questions.
6.sec: Crustal elements by abundance - most/least abundant, second-most abundant metal

6.s: Which one of the following is the most abundant metal in the Earth's crust?
6.x: Aluminium is the most abundant metal in the Earth's crust, accounting for about 8.1% by weight.
6.tq: Distinguish the most abundant element from the most abundant metal.
6.sec: Crustal elements by abundance - most/least abundant, second-most abundant metal

6.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the abundance of elements in the Earth's crust:
1. Silicon is the second-most abundant element by weight.
2. Iron is the second-most abundant metal by weight.
3. Magnesium is the least abundant among the eight major crustal elements listed.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
6.x: Silicon ranks second at about 27.7%, iron is the second-most abundant metal at about 5.0%, and magnesium ranks eighth among the listed eight elements at about 1.5%.
6.tq: Check each statement against the complete abundance ranking before selecting the coded combination.
6.sec: Crustal elements by abundance - most/least abundant, second-most abundant metal

6.s: Which one of the following correctly represents the order of major elements in the Earth as a whole by mass, from highest to lower proportion?
6.x: For the Earth as a whole, the order is iron at 32.1%, oxygen at 30.1%, silicon at 15.1% and magnesium at 13.9%.
6.tq: Separate whole-Earth composition from crustal composition and compare the first four positions.
6.sec: Crustal elements by abundance - most/least abundant, second-most abundant metal

6.s:
Which of the following pairs correctly represents Suess's chemical layers and their principal characteristics?
1. SIAL — silicon and aluminium; granitic and continental
2. SIMA — silicon and magnesium; basaltic and a source of magma
3. NIFE — nickel and iron; core with a density of about 11
Which of the statements given above are correct?
6.x: All three statements are correct. SIAL has a density of about 2.9, SIMA is basaltic and associated with magma, and NIFE forms the nickel-iron core with a density of about 11.
6.tq: Match each layer with both its chemical composition and physical character.
6.sec: Crustal elements by abundance - most/least abundant, second-most abundant metal

6.s: The scientific study of rocks is known as:
6.x: Petrology is the branch of geology concerned with the study of rocks.
6.tq: Use the exact disciplinary term rather than a related branch of Earth science.
6.sec: Rock types → examples and odd-one-out; petrology

6.s: Which one of the following groups consists entirely of sedimentary rocks?
6.x: Sandstone, limestone, shale and conglomerate are sedimentary rocks. The other groups contain igneous or metamorphic rocks.
6.tq: Classify every option by identifying the rock type of each member.
6.sec: Rock types → examples and odd-one-out; petrology

6.s: Which one of the following is the odd one out?
6.x: Marble, slate and quartzite are metamorphic rocks, whereas limestone is a sedimentary rock and a parent rock of marble.
6.tq: Identify the common rock class and then locate the parent or non-metamorphic member.
6.sec: Rock types → examples and odd-one-out; petrology

6.s: Which one of the following statements about igneous rocks is correct?
o: They are formed only through the deposition of sediments.
They are formed exclusively at the Earth's surface.
They are regarded as primary rocks formed by cooling and solidification of magma or lava.
6.x: Igneous rocks are primary rocks formed when magma or lava cools and solidifies. They generally do not contain fossils.
6.tq: Select the statement that gives both the origin and the standard classification of igneous rocks.
6.sec: Igneous - intrusive vs extrusive, felsic vs mafic

6.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Intrusive igneous rocks cool slowly at depth.
2. Slow cooling generally produces coarse grains.
3. Granite and gabbro are examples of coarse-grained intrusive rocks.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
6.x: All three statements are correct. Slow cooling within the crust permits the growth of large crystals, as seen in granite and gabbro.
6.tq: Link the setting, rate of cooling and grain size before choosing the combination.
6.sec: Igneous - intrusive vs extrusive, felsic vs mafic

6.s: Dolerite is best classified as a:
o: Fine-grained volcanic rock formed at the surface
Coarse-grained sedimentary rock formed in basins
Medium-grained hypabyssal rock occurring in dykes and sills
6.x: Dolerite is a medium-grained hypabyssal igneous rock commonly associated with dykes and sills.
6.tq: Use the location and grain-size clue to distinguish hypabyssal rocks from plutonic and volcanic rocks.
6.sec: Igneous - intrusive vs extrusive, felsic vs mafic

6.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes felsic and mafic igneous rocks?
o: Felsic rocks are generally light-coloured and silica-rich, whereas mafic rocks are generally dark-coloured and rich in iron, magnesium and calcium.
Felsic rocks are rich in iron and magnesium, whereas mafic rocks are rich in silica and aluminium.
Mafic rocks are always less dense than felsic rocks.
Both felsic and mafic rocks have identical mineral composition and colour.
6.x: Felsic rocks are silica- and feldspar-rich, generally light-coloured and of relatively low density. Mafic rocks are rich in iron, magnesium and calcium, and are generally dark and dense.
6.tq: Use the reversed-comparison trap involving colour, silica and ferromagnesian elements.
6.sec: Igneous - intrusive vs extrusive, felsic vs mafic

6.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Composition and texture)
a. Felsic intrusive
b. Felsic extrusive
c. Intermediate intrusive
d. Mafic extrusive

List-II (Rock)
i. Basalt
ii. Rhyolite
iii. Diorite
iv. Granite

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
6.x: Granite is felsic intrusive, rhyolite is felsic extrusive, diorite is intermediate intrusive and basalt is mafic extrusive.
6.tq: Start from the sure intrusive–extrusive pairs and then verify composition.
6.sec: Igneous - intrusive vs extrusive, felsic vs mafic

6.s: Which one of the following statements regarding feldspar is NOT correct?
o: Feldspar constitutes approximately one-half of the Earth's crust.
Sodium, potassium, calcium and aluminium occur in particular feldspar varieties.
Feldspar constitutes only about one-fourth of the Earth's crust.
Silicon and oxygen occur in all feldspars.
6.x: The statement that feldspar constitutes only one-fourth of the crust is incorrect. Feldspar makes up approximately half of the Earth's crust.
6.tq: Find the reversed proportion in the NOT question.
6.sec: Rock-forming minerals and silicate classes; Bowen's series; Mohs scale

6.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Mineral)
a. Muscovite
b. Albite
c. Hornblende
d. Augite

List-II (Silicate class)
i. Inosilicate — single chain
ii. Tectosilicate
iii. Phyllosilicate
iv. Inosilicate — double chain

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
6.x: Muscovite is a phyllosilicate, albite is a tectosilicate, hornblende is a double-chain inosilicate and augite is a single-chain inosilicate.
6.tq: Match minerals with their silicate structures, paying attention to single versus double chains.
6.sec: Rock-forming minerals and silicate classes; Bowen's series; Mohs scale

6.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
6.x: Olivine is a nesosilicate characterised by isolated tetrahedra. Quartz is a tectosilicate, augite is a single-chain inosilicate and hornblende is a double-chain inosilicate.
6.tq: Eliminate options by checking the structural meaning of each silicate class.
6.sec: Rock-forming minerals and silicate classes; Bowen's series; Mohs scale

6.s: In Bowen's reaction series, which mineral crystallises last from cooling magma and is regarded as the most stable among the listed minerals?
6.x: Quartz crystallises last in the stated sequence and is the most stable mineral among those listed in Bowen's reaction series.
6.tq: Use the endpoint of the crystallisation sequence rather than its first high-temperature mineral.
6.sec: Rock-forming minerals and silicate classes; Bowen's series; Mohs scale

6.s:
Arrange the following minerals in the order in which they crystallise in the discontinuous branch of Bowen's reaction series, from earliest to latest:
A. Biotite
B. Olivine
C. Amphibole
D. Pyroxene
6.x: The discontinuous branch proceeds from olivine to pyroxene, amphibole and biotite as magma cools.
6.tq: Identify the first high-temperature mineral and follow the standard branch sequence.
6.sec: Rock-forming minerals and silicate classes; Bowen's series; Mohs scale

6.s: Which one of the following correctly represents the continuous branch of Bowen's reaction series?
6.x: The continuous branch involves the progressive change from calcium-rich plagioclase to sodium-rich plagioclase during cooling.
6.tq: Discriminate between the continuous plagioclase branch and the discontinuous ferromagnesian branch.
6.sec: Rock-forming minerals and silicate classes; Bowen's series; Mohs scale

6.s: Which of the following is the correct order of minerals on the Mohs hardness scale from 1 to 4?
6.x: The first four minerals on the Mohs scale are talc, gypsum, calcite and fluorite, with hardness values from 1 to 4 respectively.
6.tq: Preserve the exact ascending order in a short numerical sequence.
6.sec: Rock-forming minerals and silicate classes; Bowen's series; Mohs scale

6.s: Which mineral has a Mohs hardness of 7?
6.x: Quartz has a Mohs hardness of 7. Orthoclase is 6, topaz is 8 and apatite is 5.
6.tq: Use the central value in the hardness scale and distinguish neighbouring entries.
6.sec: Rock-forming minerals and silicate classes; Bowen's series; Mohs scale

6.s: Which one of the following represents the correct upper end of the Mohs hardness scale?
6.x: The scale progresses from quartz at 7 to topaz at 8, corundum at 9 and diamond at 10.
6.tq: Arrange the final members by increasing hardness and verify the endpoint.
6.sec: Rock-forming minerals and silicate classes; Bowen's series; Mohs scale

6.s: Which one of the following statements about quartz is correct?
o: It is a double-chain inosilicate found only in basalt.
It is the first mineral to crystallise from cooling magma.
It is a soft mineral that weathers very rapidly and is absent from sandstone.
It is composed of silicon dioxide and forms a major part of granite and sandstone.
6.x: Quartz is silicon dioxide (SiO2), is relatively hard and resistant to weathering, and is a major component of granite and sandstone.
6.tq: Combine chemical composition, resistance to weathering and occurrence in the precise option.
6.sec: Rock-forming minerals and silicate classes; Bowen's series; Mohs scale

6.s: Which one of the following statements about volcanic rocks is correct?
o: All volcanic rocks are coarse-grained because lava cools slowly at depth.
Andesite, dacite, rhyolite and basalt generally require more energy to fracture than many sedimentary rocks.
Volcanic rocks are formed only by sediment deposition.
Volcanic rocks necessarily contain abundant fossils.
6.x: Andesite, dacite, rhyolite and basalt are volcanic rocks, and they generally require more energy to fracture than many sedimentary rocks. They usually cool rapidly and are fine-grained.
6.tq: Reject absolute statements and focus on the stated mechanical comparison.
6.sec: Igneous - intrusive vs extrusive, felsic vs mafic

6.s: Which one of the following rock types is the principal host of fossils, coal, petroleum and natural gas?
6.x: Sedimentary rocks commonly preserve fossils and host coal, petroleum and natural gas.
6.tq: Directly identify the rock type associated with fossils and fossil fuels.
6.sec: Fossils and fossil fuels by rock type

6.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Sandstone may contain plant, animal and microorganism fossils.
2. Sedimentary rocks are associated with coal, petroleum and natural gas.
3. Igneous rocks are the principal repositories of fossils.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
6.x: Sandstone and other sedimentary rocks may preserve fossils and contain fossil fuels. Igneous rocks are not the principal repositories of fossils.
6.tq: Find the statement that reverses the usual fossil-bearing character of rocks.
6.sec: Fossils and fossil fuels by rock type

6.s: The description of Archaean rocks as a ‘no fossils’ zone is primarily associated with which of the following reasons?
o: They were subjected to recent volcanic eruptions
They were formed before the emergence of life
They were formed only in oceanic trenches
6.x: Archaean rocks formed before life appeared and therefore are regarded as a no-fossils zone.
6.tq: Link the geological age of a rock system with the reason for absence of fossils.
6.sec: Fossils and fossil fuels by rock type

6.s: Which of the following correctly distinguishes Dravidian rocks from Archaean rocks with respect to fossils?
o: Archaean rocks are fossil-rich, whereas Dravidian rocks contain no fossils
Only igneous varieties of both systems contain fossils
Dravidian rocks are fossil-rich, whereas Archaean rocks are generally devoid of fossils
Both are generally devoid of fossils
6.x: Dravidian or Palaeozoic rocks contain abundant marine fossils, while Archaean rocks formed before life and generally contain none.
6.tq: Use the reversed-comparison trap in a two-system distinction.
6.sec: Fossils and fossil fuels by rock type

6.s: Approximately what proportion of India’s coal is held by the Gondwana rocks?
6.x: Gondwana rocks hold nearly 98 percent of India’s coal.
6.tq: Test the distinctive percentage directly using close numerical distractors.
6.sec: Fossils and fossil fuels by rock type

6.s:
With reference to Gondwana and Carboniferous coal, consider the following statements:
1. Gondwana coal is younger than Carboniferous coal.
2. Gondwana coal contains less carbon than Carboniferous coal.
3. Gondwana coal is found only in the Himalayan region.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
6.x: Gondwana coal is younger and has a lower carbon content than Carboniferous coal. It is not confined to the Himalayas.
6.tq: Separate two linked comparative facts from a false location claim.
6.sec: Fossils and fossil fuels by rock type

6.s: Mount Everest is composed primarily of which of the following?
6.x: Mount Everest is described as being composed of Upper Carboniferous limestone.
6.tq: Directly test a distinctive rock–landform association.
6.sec: Fossils and fossil fuels by rock type

6.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
6.x: Granite metamorphoses into gneiss. Limestone forms marble, coal forms graphite and sandstone forms quartzite.
6.tq: Start from the sure parent-to-metamorphic-rock pair.
6.sec: Metamorphic - parent → metamorphosed rock; typical minerals

6.s: Clay or shale, when subjected to metamorphism, generally gives rise first to which rock?
6.x: Clay or shale metamorphoses into slate; with further metamorphism, slate may develop into schist.
6.tq: Discriminate between closely related metamorphic products.
6.sec: Metamorphic - parent → metamorphosed rock; typical minerals

6.s: Coal undergoes progressive metamorphism through anthracite and ultimately forms which metamorphic rock?
6.x: Coal may pass through anthracite during metamorphism and ultimately form graphite.
6.tq: Test the sequence rather than merely the end product.
6.sec: Metamorphic - parent → metamorphosed rock; typical minerals

6.s: Which of the following is NOT a typical metamorphic mineral?
6.x: Garnet, kyanite and sillimanite are typical metamorphic minerals. Halite is associated with chemically formed sedimentary deposits.
6.tq: Find the odd mineral from a nearby sedimentary category.
6.sec: Metamorphic - parent → metamorphosed rock; typical minerals

6.s: Metamorphic rocks are generally formed when pre-existing rocks undergo:
o: Recrystallisation under heat and pressure without melting
Deposition and cementation at the Earth’s surface
Complete melting followed by rapid cooling
6.x: Metamorphism involves recrystallisation under heat and pressure, without complete melting of the rock.
6.tq: Use the key distinction between metamorphism and melting.
6.sec: Metamorphic - parent → metamorphosed rock; typical minerals

6.s: Which one of the following pairs of processes represents the two broad types of metamorphism mentioned in relation to heat, pressure and deformation?
o: Thermal or contact, and regional or dynamic
6.x: Thermal or contact metamorphism and regional or dynamic metamorphism are the broad forms identified in this classification.
6.tq: Distinguish metamorphic processes from sedimentary modes of formation.
6.sec: Metamorphic - parent → metamorphosed rock; typical minerals

6.s:
Consider the following statements about metamorphism:
1. Both igneous and sedimentary rocks may undergo metamorphism.
2. Metamorphism necessarily involves complete melting.
3. Heat and pressure are important agents of metamorphism.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
6.x: Igneous and sedimentary rocks can become metamorphic under heat and pressure. Complete melting is not required and would lead toward magma formation.
6.tq: Reject the absolute statement that confuses metamorphism with melting.
6.sec: Metamorphic - parent → metamorphosed rock; typical minerals

6.s: Which one of the following groups contains only metamorphic rocks?
o: Coal, rock salt, gypsum and conglomerate
Marble, slate, quartzite, gneiss and schist
6.x: Marble, slate, quartzite, gneiss and schist are metamorphic rocks.
6.tq: Classify the complete group rather than one isolated example.
6.sec: Metamorphic - parent → metamorphosed rock; typical minerals

6.s: Sedimentary rocks are called ‘stratified rocks’ because they are generally formed as:
o: Successive layers of deposited, compacted and cemented sediments
Single layers of volcanic ash only
Metamorphosed rocks melted beneath the crust
6.x: Sediments are transported, deposited, compacted and cemented into successive layers called strata.
6.tq: Connect the descriptive term with its formation process.
6.sec: Sedimentary rocks - formation, stratification, porosity vs permeability

6.s: Which sequence correctly represents the principal stages in the formation of a sedimentary rock from broken rock material?
6.x: Broken rock material is transported and deposited, then compacted and cemented to form sedimentary rock.
6.tq: Arrange the formation stages in their natural order.
6.sec: Sedimentary rocks - formation, stratification, porosity vs permeability

6.s: Which one of the following is correctly classified as a mechanically formed sedimentary rock?
6.x: Conglomerate is mechanically or clastically formed. Rock salt and gypsum are chemically formed, while geyserite is organically classified here.
6.tq: Match the formation mode with its characteristic example.
6.sec: Sedimentary rocks - formation, stratification, porosity vs permeability

6.s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I (Mode of formation)
 a. Mechanically formed
 b. Chemically formed
 c. Organically formed

List-II (Example)
 i. Coal
 ii. Rock salt
 iii. Sandstone

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
6.x: Sandstone is mechanically formed, rock salt is chemically formed and coal is organically formed.
6.tq: Start from the sure pair and eliminate codes with swapped formation modes.
6.sec: Sedimentary rocks - formation, stratification, porosity vs permeability

6.s: Which one of the following is an organically formed sedimentary rock?
6.x: Chalk is classified as an organically formed sedimentary rock. Chert and halite are chemically formed, while loess is mechanically formed.
6.tq: Use the source of material to distinguish organic from chemical and clastic rocks.
6.sec: Sedimentary rocks - formation, stratification, porosity vs permeability

6.s: In geological terminology, porosity refers to the:
o: Amount of pore space present in a rock
Ability of a rock to transmit water
Rate at which a rock melts
Resistance of a rock to weathering
6.x: Porosity is the amount or proportion of pore space in a rock. Permeability refers to the ability to allow water to pass through it.
6.tq: Discriminate between the paired terms porosity and permeability.
6.sec: Sedimentary rocks - formation, stratification, porosity vs permeability

6.s: Which one of the following correctly describes clay with respect to porosity and permeability?
6.x: Clay contains pore spaces but its very fine particles prevent the easy passage of water; hence it is porous but impermeable.
6.tq: Test the difference between having pore space and transmitting water.
6.sec: Sedimentary rocks - formation, stratification, porosity vs permeability

6.s: Which one of the following rocks is generally neither porous nor permeable?
6.x: Chalk and sandstone are porous and permeable, clay is porous but impermeable, whereas granite is generally neither porous nor permeable.
6.tq: Compare all four rock behaviours before selecting the exception.
6.sec: Sedimentary rocks - formation, stratification, porosity vs permeability

6.s: A rock contains pore spaces and also permits water to pass through them. Which pair best fits this description?
6.x: Chalk and sandstone are described as both porous and permeable.
6.tq: Apply the definitions of porosity and permeability to a practical description.
6.sec: Sedimentary rocks - formation, stratification, porosity vs permeability

6.s: Which one of the following statements about sedimentary rocks is correct?
o: They are formed exclusively below the mantle by melting
They may contain fossils because sediments can preserve remains during deposition and lithification
They are always non-layered and crystalline
They cannot be formed from pre-existing rock fragments
6.x: Sedimentary rocks form from deposited sediments and may preserve fossils within the resulting layers.
6.tq: Choose the careful, process-based statement over absolute claims.
6.sec: Sedimentary rocks - formation, stratification, porosity vs permeability

6.s: Which sequence correctly represents the broad rock cycle beginning with exposed rock material at the surface?
o: Weathering and erosion → deposition and lithification → heat and pressure → melting
Heat and pressure → weathering → crystallisation → deposition
6.x: Surface rocks undergo weathering, erosion, transportation and deposition; lithification forms sedimentary rocks, heat and pressure form metamorphic rocks, and melting produces magma.
6.tq: Follow the process chain from the surface toward the interior.
6.sec: Rock cycle - processes linking the three types

6.s: Which process changes sedimentary rock into metamorphic rock in the rock cycle?
o: Heat and pressure during deeper burial
6.x: Deeper burial subjects sedimentary rocks to heat and pressure, causing metamorphism.
6.tq: Identify the process linking two adjacent rock types.
6.sec: Rock cycle - processes linking the three types

6.s: In the rock cycle, the immediate product of melting a metamorphic rock is:
6.x: Melting converts metamorphic rock into magma, which may later cool to form igneous rock.
6.tq: Test the reversible link between metamorphic rock and magma.
6.sec: Rock cycle - processes linking the three types

6.s:
Consider the following statements about the rock cycle:
1. Any rock type can, under suitable conditions, be transformed into any other rock type.
2. Exposed metamorphic rocks can weather and become sediment.
3. Igneous rocks can form only from sedimentary rocks.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
6.x: Any rock may enter different pathways in the rock cycle, and exposed metamorphic rocks can weather into sediment. Igneous rocks are not formed only from sedimentary rocks.
6.tq: Reject the exclusive claim while retaining the general-cycle statements.
6.sec: Rock cycle - processes linking the three types

6.s: Carbon dioxide dissolved in rainwater contributes to weathering by forming:
6.x: Carbon dioxide in rainwater forms carbonic acid, which helps weather rocks.
6.tq: Test the chemical agent involved in carbon cycling and weathering.
6.sec: Rock cycle - processes linking the three types

6.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the storage of carbon through weathering?
o: Carbon is converted only into atmospheric oxygen
Carbon is stored exclusively in igneous crystals
Weathering can help store carbon as bicarbonate and limestone
Carbon is permanently removed only through volcanic eruptions
6.x: Carbonic acid weathering can carry carbon as bicarbonate, which may later become stored in limestone.
6.tq: Apply the carbon-cycle connection to the weathering process.
6.sec: Rock cycle - processes linking the three types

6.s: Rock material brought up from the mantle during eruptions is most directly associated with the formation of:
6.x: Mantle material reaching the surface as magma or lava cools and forms igneous rocks.
6.tq: Link volcanic mantle material with its immediate rock product.
6.sec: Rock cycle - processes linking the three types

6.s: What generally happens to subducted crust in the deeper mantle?
o: It melts back into the mantle
6.x: Subducted crust may melt back into the mantle, contributing to the continuing rock cycle.
6.tq: Use the direction of plate movement and depth-related process as the clue.
6.sec: Rock cycle - processes linking the three types

6.s: Which Indian rock system is older than 2,500 million years and forms the oldest crustal core of the Indian craton?
6.x: The Archaean system is older than 2,500 million years and constitutes the oldest crustal core of the Indian craton.
6.tq: Identify the system from its distinctive age and geological role.
6.sec: Rock systems of India - composition and what each holds

6.s: Which one of the following combinations is characteristic of the Archaean rock system?
o: Granites, gneisses and schists; no fossils
6.x: Archaean rocks include granites, gneisses and schists and are generally devoid of fossils.
6.tq: Match composition and fossil character with the correct geological system.
6.sec: Rock systems of India - composition and what each holds

6.s: The Dharwar system is regarded as economically the most important mainly because it contains significant deposits of:
o: Coal, chalk and coral limestone only

7.s:
Arrange the following events in chronological order from earliest to latest:
A. Break-up of Gondwanaland
B. Rise of the Himalayas
C. Separation of the Peninsular Plateau from Africa during the Cretaceous
D. Proposal of continental drift by Wegener

In the broad geological sequence represented here, the intended order is A, C, D, B.
7.tq: Arrange geological events by separating deep-time events from the dated scientific proposal and Himalayan uplift.
7.sec: Gondwanaland vs Laurasia - present landmasses; India's parent landmass

7.x: After the breakup of Gondwanaland, the Indian craton moved northwards towards the Eurasian craton.
7.tq: Test the direction and destination of continental movement.

7.s: The theory of plate tectonics was put together in 1967 by McKenzie and Parker and independently by:
7.x: McKenzie and Parker developed the theory in 1967, and Morgan proposed it independently.

7.s: The lithospheric plates float on the:
7.x: The rigid lithosphere is broken into plates that float on the semi-fluid asthenosphere.
7.tq: Distinguish the rigid layer from the underlying semi-fluid layer.

7.s: Which one of the following is NOT one of the seven major plates listed in plate tectonics?
7.x: The seven listed major plates are Pacific, North American, South American, Eurasian, African, Indo-Australian and Antarctic. Nazca is a minor plate.
7.tq: Separate a minor plate from the standard list of major plates.
7.sec: Plate tectonics - proponents, major and minor plates, monitoring

7.s: Which of the following groups contains only major plates?
7.x: Pacific, Eurasian, African and Antarctic are among the seven major plates. The other groups contain minor plates.
7.tq: Classify every item in the group before selecting the complete set.
7.sec: Plate tectonics - proponents, major and minor plates, monitoring

7.s: The Nazca Plate lies between the:
7.x: The Nazca Plate is located between the South American Plate and the Pacific Plate.
7.tq: Test a minor plate by its bordering major plates.
7.sec: Plate tectonics - proponents, major and minor plates, monitoring

7.s: The Caroline Plate is located:
o: Between the Philippine and Indian plates, north of New Guinea
Between Central America and the Pacific Plate
Mostly over the Saudi Arabian landmass
Between South America and the Pacific Plate
7.x: The Caroline Plate lies between the Philippine and Indian plates and is situated north of New Guinea.
7.tq: Use both bordering plates and the regional location for precise identification.
7.sec: Plate tectonics - proponents, major and minor plates, monitoring

7.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
o: Philippine Plate — between the Asiatic and Pacific plates
Arabian Plate — between South America and the Pacific Plate
Caribbean Plate — north of New Guinea between Philippine and Indian plates
Cocos Plate — mostly the Saudi Arabian landmass
7.x: The Philippine Plate lies between the Asiatic and Pacific plates. The Arabian, Caribbean and Cocos descriptions in the other options are incorrect.
7.tq: Identify the correct minor-plate location while rejecting swapped descriptions.
7.sec: Plate tectonics - proponents, major and minor plates, monitoring

7.s: The Cocos Plate subducts under the Caribbean Plate, a process associated with:
7.x: The Cocos Plate subducts beneath the Caribbean Plate, and this setting is associated with Volcan de Fuego.
7.tq: Link a plate interaction with its named volcanic example.
7.sec: Plate tectonics - proponents, major and minor plates, monitoring

7.s: The Caribbean Plate borders the South American Plate, and Venezuela lies on this boundary. Which statement is correct?
o: The Caribbean Plate is located entirely within the Pacific Ocean.
Venezuela is associated with the boundary between the Caribbean and South American plates.
The Caribbean Plate lies north of New Guinea between the Indian and Philippine plates.
The Caribbean Plate is one of the seven major plates.
7.x: The Caribbean Plate borders the South American Plate, and Venezuela lies on this boundary. The Caribbean Plate is a minor plate.
7.tq: Apply the boundary relationship to the named country.
7.sec: Plate tectonics - proponents, major and minor plates, monitoring

7.s: Arthur Holmes is associated with the explanation that plate movements are driven by:
7.x: Arthur Holmes proposed mantle convection as a driving mechanism for plate movement.
7.tq: Match the scientist with the mechanism rather than with the original drift forces.
7.sec: Plate tectonics - proponents, major and minor plates, monitoring

7.s: Which instrument-based method is used to monitor plate movement?
7.x: Plate movement is monitored using GPS data.
7.tq: Distinguish the modern monitoring technology from unrelated instruments.
7.sec: Plate tectonics - proponents, major and minor plates, monitoring

7.s: The Geological Survey of India has how many GNSS stations for tracking crustal movement and building strain models?
7.x: The Geological Survey of India has 34 GNSS stations for monitoring crustal movement and developing strain models.
7.tq: Recall the exact institutional network count.
7.sec: Plate tectonics - proponents, major and minor plates, monitoring

7.s:
Consider the following statements about plate boundaries:
1. At a divergent boundary, plates move apart and new crust forms.
2. At a convergent boundary, collision or subduction may occur.
3. At a transform boundary, plates slide past each other.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
7.x: All three statements correctly describe divergent, convergent and transform boundaries respectively.
7.tq: Use the motion-based definitions to identify the complete correct set.
7.sec: Plate tectonics - proponents, major and minor plates, monitoring

7.s: Which of the following is correctly matched with a divergent or constructive boundary?
o: Andes — plates move apart without subduction
Himalayas — plates slide horizontally past each other
Mid-Atlantic Ridge — plates move apart and new crust forms
San Andreas Fault — new crust forms by seafloor spreading
7.x: Divergent boundaries involve plates moving apart and the formation of new crust; the Mid-Atlantic Ridge is an example.
7.tq: Match the boundary type with both its motion and landform.
7.sec: Plate tectonics - proponents, major and minor plates, monitoring

7.s: The Himalayas are an example of a landform associated with a:
o: Divergent boundary between two oceanic plates
Convergent boundary between the Indian and Eurasian plates
Transform boundary between the Pacific and Nazca plates
Constructive boundary between the African and Indian plates
7.x: The Himalayas formed at the convergent boundary where the Indian Plate collides with the Eurasian Plate.
7.tq: Connect a major landform with the correct plate interaction.
7.sec: Plate tectonics - proponents, major and minor plates, monitoring

7.s: Which one of the following sets contains only features associated with convergent boundaries?
o: Trenches, island arcs and the Andes
Mid-Atlantic Ridge, rift valleys and San Andreas Fault
Rift valleys, trenches and transform faults
San Andreas Fault, Sagaing Fault and Mid-Atlantic Ridge
7.x: Convergent boundaries involve collision or subduction and may produce trenches, island arcs and the Andes.
7.tq: Classify landforms by the plate-boundary process that produces them.
7.sec: Plate tectonics - proponents, major and minor plates, monitoring

7.s: The San Andreas Fault is an example of a:
7.x: The San Andreas Fault is a transform boundary where plates slide past each other.
7.tq: Discriminate among the three boundary types using the characteristic motion.
7.sec: Plate tectonics - proponents, major and minor plates, monitoring

7.s: The Sagaing Fault in Myanmar is described as a transform boundary between the:
7.x: The Sagaing Fault is a conservative or transform boundary between the Indian and Eurasian plates.
7.tq: Match a named fault with the plates on either side.
7.sec: Plate tectonics - proponents, major and minor plates, monitoring

7.s: Who proposed the sea-floor spreading hypothesis in the early 1960s?
7.x: Harry Hess proposed the sea-floor spreading hypothesis in the early 1960s, including the creation of new crust at mid-ocean ridges and its destruction at trenches.
7.tq: Use direct person–theory identification and distinguish the proponent from related plate-tectonic thinkers.
7.sec: Sea-floor spreading - proponent, palaeomagnetism, crust age and thickness  [APPSC]

7.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the process of sea-floor spreading?
o: Oceanic crust remains stationary while only the continents move over it.
Magma rises at mid-ocean ridges, creates new oceanic crust and pushes older crust sideways.
Continental crust sinks at ridges and produces new oceanic sediments.
Magma rises at trenches, creates continental crust and moves toward the ridges.
7.x: At mid-ocean ridges, rising magma forms new oceanic crust and pushes the existing crust sideways; older crust is eventually destroyed at trenches.
7.tq: Test the mechanism through a process-based scenario and reject reversed source-and-destination relationships.
7.sec: Sea-floor spreading - proponent, palaeomagnetism, crust age and thickness  [APPSC]

7.s:
Consider the following statements regarding palaeomagnetism:
1. Rocks at mid-ocean ridges preserve the magnetic field of the time when they formed.
2. Normal and reversed magnetic polarity bands occur symmetrically on either side of a ridge.
3. Palaeomagnetic evidence indicates that all oceanic crust formed during one period of normal polarity.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
7.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Ocean-floor rocks record alternating normal and reversed magnetic polarity, so statement 3 is incorrect.
7.tq: Find the single exaggerated statement among closely related palaeomagnetic facts.
7.sec: Sea-floor spreading - proponent, palaeomagnetism, crust age and thickness  [APPSC]

7.s: The symmetrical bands of normal and reversed magnetic polarity on either side of a mid-ocean ridge were especially explained by the work of
7.x: Vine and Matthews explained the symmetrical magnetic stripes as evidence supporting sea-floor spreading in 1963.
7.tq: Use a contributor–evidence association question to distinguish supporting researchers from the principal proposer.
7.sec: Sea-floor spreading - proponent, palaeomagnetism, crust age and thickness  [APPSC]

7.s: The Brunhes–Matuyama magnetic reversal occurred approximately
7.x: The Brunhes–Matuyama reversal is dated to approximately 780,000 years ago.
7.tq: Test the order of magnitude carefully by separating thousand, million and larger time scales.
7.sec: Sea-floor spreading - proponent, palaeomagnetism, crust age and thickness  [APPSC]

7.s: Moving away from a mid-ocean ridge, which one of the following trends is observed in oceanic crust and its sediment cover?
o: Age increases, while density and thickness decrease.
Only sediment thickness increases; crustal age and density remain unchanged.
Age, density and thickness decrease continuously.
7.x: The age, density and thickness of oceanic crust, along with the thickness of its sediment cover, increase with distance from the ridge.
7.tq: Apply the directional trend rule by comparing conditions near the ridge with those farther away.
7.sec: Sea-floor spreading - proponent, palaeomagnetism, crust age and thickness  [APPSC]

7.s: Which one of the following statements about oceanic crust is correct?
o: Its oldest portions are about 200 million years old and are much younger than continental rocks.
It is generally older than continental crust.
It is nowhere younger than 200 million years.
Its age is unrelated to its distance from a mid-ocean ridge.
7.x: Oceanic crust is far younger than continental crust, and the oldest ocean-floor rocks are approximately 200 million years old.
7.tq: Discriminate between the relative ages of oceanic and continental crust and identify the correct upper-age estimate.
7.sec: Sea-floor spreading - proponent, palaeomagnetism, crust age and thickness  [APPSC]

7.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Feature)

 b. Himalaya
 c. Andes
 d. San Andreas Fault

 i. Transform boundary
 ii. Convergent ocean–continent boundary

 iv. Convergent continent–continent boundary

7.s: The Red Sea and the East African Rift are associated with

collision of the Indian and Eurasian plates
horizontal sliding of the Pacific and North American plates
subduction of the Nazca Plate beneath the South American Plate

7.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Andes — Nazca Plate subducting beneath the South American Plate

7.s:
Which of the following statements about earthquakes at plate boundaries are correct?
1. Stretching and fracturing can produce earthquakes at divergent boundaries.
2. Friction associated with subduction can produce earthquakes at convergent boundaries.
3. Sudden slip along horizontally moving plates can produce earthquakes at transform boundaries.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
7.x: Earthquakes occur at all three major boundary types: through stretching at divergent boundaries, subduction-related friction at convergent boundaries, and sudden slip at transform boundaries.
7.tq: Check whether the same natural hazard can arise through different mechanisms at all three boundary types.
7.sec: Plate boundaries - example → type  [other exams]

7.s: The Indian Plate has generally drifted in which direction since its separation from the southern landmass?
o: Westward, parallel to the African coast
Northward, from a position far south of the equator

7.tq: Use the directional movement and past-position pair rather than testing direction alone.

7.s: The Deccan Traps were erupted while the Indian Plate was
o: crossing near the equator and passing over the Reunion hotspot
moving southward across the Tethys Sea
colliding with the Eurasian Plate in the Himalaya
7.x: The Deccan Traps erupted as the northward-moving Indian Plate crossed near the equator and passed over the Reunion hotspot.
7.tq: Connect a geological event with the plate’s position and hotspot passage at that time.
7.sec: Indian plate - drift direction, rate, collision history  [other exams]

7.s: At approximately what rate is the Indian Plate currently moving northward into the Eurasian Plate?

7.sec: Indian plate - drift direction, rate, collision history  [other exams]

7.sec: Indian plate - drift direction, rate, collision history  [other exams]

7.s: The collision between the Indian and Eurasian plates began approximately
7.x: The collision began approximately 4–5 crore years ago, equivalent to about 40–50 million years ago. Some older estimates place it at about 50–55 million years ago.
7.tq: Convert crore-based geological time into its equivalent million-year scale without changing the order of magnitude.
7.sec: Indian plate - drift direction, rate, collision history  [other exams]

7.s: Which sequence correctly describes the principal geological consequences of the Indian–Eurasian collision?
o: Formation of the Atlantic Ocean, followed by subduction beneath Africa
Separation of India from Eurasia and formation of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge
Opening of the Tethys, subsidence of its sediments and formation of oceanic ridges
Closure of the Tethys, folding and thrusting of its sediments, and uplift of the Himalaya
7.x: The collision closed the Tethys Sea; its sediments were folded and thrust upward to form the Himalaya, which continues to rise.
7.tq: Follow the cause–effect chain and reject options that reverse convergence into divergence.
7.sec: Indian plate - drift direction, rate, collision history  [other exams]

7.s: Which one of the following is the correct north-to-south sequence of major Himalayan structural zones?
o: Indus–Tsangpo Suture, Main Central Thrust, Main Boundary Thrust, Himalayan Frontal Fault
Himalayan Frontal Fault, Main Boundary Thrust, Main Central Thrust, Indus–Tsangpo Suture
Main Central Thrust, Indus–Tsangpo Suture, Himalayan Frontal Fault, Main Boundary Thrust
Main Boundary Thrust, Himalayan Frontal Fault, Indus–Tsangpo Suture, Main Central Thrust
7.x: The principal structural zones are arranged from north to south as the Indus–Tsangpo Suture, Main Central Thrust, Main Boundary Thrust and Himalayan Frontal Fault.
7.tq: Use spatial ordering from the northern suture toward the southern frontal fault.
7.sec: Indian plate - drift direction, rate, collision history  [other exams]

7.s: The underthrusting of India beneath Asia between approximately 45 and 20 million years ago contributed particularly to the uplift of the
7.x: India underthrust Asia between about 45 and 20 million years ago, helping to lift the Tibetan Plateau.
7.tq: Associate the stated time interval with the specific plateau uplift caused by underthrusting.
7.sec: Indian plate - drift direction, rate, collision history  [other exams]

7.s: The western part of Tibet is considered more rugged because the Indian Plate
o: formed a transform boundary with the Arabian Plate
was completely subducted beneath the Pacific Plate
moved away from western Tibet toward the Indian Ocean
7.x: The Indian Plate pushed deeper beneath western Tibet, contributing to the greater ruggedness of that region.
