17.s: Which one of the following correctly describes convectional precipitation?
o: Moist air is forced up a mountain slope and descends dry on the leeward side.
Warm air is lifted over cold air along a front.
Strong surface heating causes air to rise, cool and condense, often producing afternoon showers.
Rainfall results exclusively from the movement of ocean currents.
17.x: Convectional precipitation develops when intense heating causes air to rise, cool and condense, commonly producing afternoon showers and thunderstorms.
17.tq: Identify the precipitation type from its initiating mechanism rather than its location alone.
17.sec: Precipitation types - convectional, orographic, cyclonic/frontal  [APPSC]

17.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Equatorial regions may receive convectional rain almost every day throughout the year.
2. Pre-monsoon mango showers are an example of convectional precipitation.
3. Convectional precipitation is caused by warm air being lifted over cold air along a front.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
17.x: Equatorial daily rainfall and pre-monsoon mango showers are examples of convectional precipitation. Warm air rising over cold air along a front describes frontal precipitation, not convectional precipitation.
17.tq: Separate heating-driven uplift from frontal uplift when evaluating the statements.
17.sec: Precipitation types - convectional, orographic, cyclonic/frontal  [APPSC]

17.s: Orographic precipitation occurs when
o: air rises only because of intense heating over an ocean
cold air sinks below warm air in the lower atmosphere
dry air descends on the windward slope of a mountain
moist air is forced to rise over a mountain barrier
17.x: Orographic precipitation results when moist winds are forced upward over a mountain or other relief barrier.
17.tq: Identify the relief-based mechanism and distinguish it from convectional and frontal uplift.
17.sec: Precipitation types - convectional, orographic, cyclonic/frontal  [APPSC]

17.s:
With reference to orographic rainfall, consider the following statements:
1. The windward side of a mountain generally receives heavier rainfall.
2. The leeward side may lie in a rain shadow.
3. Agumbe and Hulikal are associated with the wet Western Ghats.
4. Rayalaseema lies in the rain-shadow region in the stated monsoon setting.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
17.x: Moist air produces heavier rainfall on the windward side, while the leeward side is drier. Agumbe and Hulikal are wet Western Ghats locations, and Rayalaseema is identified as lying in the rain shadow in the stated setting.
17.tq: Combine the physical rule with the location-based examples before selecting the complete code.
17.sec: Precipitation types - convectional, orographic, cyclonic/frontal  [APPSC]

17.s: Which one of the following locations is identified as the driest place in India, with approximately 8.33 cm of rainfall?
17.x: Ruyli in Jaisalmer is identified as the driest place in India, receiving approximately 8.33 cm of rainfall.
17.tq: Use the location–rainfall extreme pair and distinguish the dry extreme from wet-region examples.
17.sec: Precipitation types - convectional, orographic, cyclonic/frontal  [APPSC]

17.s: The rainfall at Mawsynram is most directly associated with which type of precipitation?
o: Frontal precipitation caused by western disturbances
Cyclonic precipitation caused only by temperate cyclones
17.x: Mawsynram receives exceptional rainfall due primarily to the orographic lifting of moist winds over relief.
17.tq: Apply the relief mechanism to a well-known high-rainfall location.
17.sec: Precipitation types - convectional, orographic, cyclonic/frontal  [APPSC]

17.s: Cyclonic or frontal precipitation is best described as precipitation in which
o: warm air is lifted over cold air along a front or air rises in a cyclone’s low-pressure centre
moist air descends on the windward side of a mountain
air rises only after intense heating over an equatorial landmass
rainfall is produced exclusively by cloud seeding
17.x: Cyclonic or frontal precipitation occurs when warm air rises over cold air along fronts or when air rises in a cyclone’s low-pressure centre.
17.tq: Match the precipitation type with its defining uplift mechanism and avoid absolute distractors.
17.sec: Precipitation types - convectional, orographic, cyclonic/frontal  [APPSC]

17.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Western disturbances — 10–15 cm winter precipitation in north-western India
Mango showers — frontal precipitation in temperate belts
Ruyli — wettest location of the Western Ghats
17.x: Western disturbances can provide about 10–15 cm of precipitation to north-western India, benefiting rabi crops. The other pairs reverse or misstate the geographical associations.
17.tq: Start from the distinctive rainfall amount and then eliminate reversed location–phenomenon pairs.
17.sec: Precipitation types - convectional, orographic, cyclonic/frontal  [APPSC]

17.s: In the context of the south-west monsoon, which of the following regions is identified as lying in its rain shadow?
o: Only the windward slopes of the Western Ghats
Maharashtra, Karnataka, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh and the interiors of Tamil Nadu
Only the coastal districts of Kerala
17.x: After crossing the Western Ghats, the stated rain-shadow region includes Maharashtra, Karnataka, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh and the interiors of Tamil Nadu.
17.tq: Use the windward–leeward relationship to identify the grouped rain-shadow regions.
17.sec: Precipitation types - convectional, orographic, cyclonic/frontal  [APPSC]

17.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes the examples of precipitation types?
o: Equatorial afternoon showers—cyclonic; Western Ghats rainfall—convectional; Bay of Bengal cyclones—orographic
Equatorial afternoon showers—convectional; Western Ghats rainfall—orographic; Bay of Bengal cyclones—cyclonic
All three examples represent frontal precipitation
Equatorial afternoon showers—orographic; Western Ghats rainfall—cyclonic; Bay of Bengal cyclones—convectional
17.x: Equatorial and summer-interior afternoon showers are convectional, Western Ghats rainfall is orographic, and Bay of Bengal cyclones produce cyclonic precipitation.
17.tq: Classify each example by its initiating mechanism rather than by the amount of rainfall.
17.sec: Precipitation types - convectional, orographic, cyclonic/frontal  [APPSC]

17.s: Which one of the following is NOT a process of the hydrological cycle?
17.x: Photosynthesis is a biological process and is not a stage of the hydrological cycle. Transpiration, percolation and surface runoff are components of the cycle.
17.tq: Find the process that does not belong to the cycle.
17.sec: Hydrological cycle - processes that belong and those that do not; hydrometeorology  [APPSC]

17.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the hydrological cycle:
1. Evapotranspiration combines evaporation and transpiration.
2. Sublimation can form part of the hydrological cycle.
3. Groundwater flow is included in the movement of water through the cycle.
4. Combustion is a normal stage of the hydrological cycle.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
17.x: Evapotranspiration, sublimation and groundwater flow are components of the hydrological cycle. Combustion is not a stage of the cycle.
17.tq: Separate the listed cycle processes from the biological or unrelated distractor.
17.sec: Hydrological cycle - processes that belong and those that do not; hydrometeorology  [APPSC]

17.s: Hydrometeorology is primarily concerned with the study of
o: the transfer of water and energy between the land surface and the lower atmosphere
the movement of tectonic plates beneath the oceans
the chemical composition of ocean water alone
the geological evolution of mountain ranges
17.x: Hydrometeorology studies the transfer of water and energy between the land surface and the lower atmosphere, including rainfall, floods and droughts.
17.tq: Match the specialised discipline with its exact field of study.
17.sec: Hydrological cycle - processes that belong and those that do not; hydrometeorology  [APPSC]

17.s: Which one of the following correctly represents the approximate annual water balance of India given in the data?
o: Precipitation 4,000 BCM; natural runoff after evaporation 1,139 BCM; utilisable water 2,000 BCM
Precipitation 1,999.20 BCM; natural runoff after evaporation 4,000 BCM; utilisable water 690 BCM
Precipitation 4,000 BCM; natural runoff after evaporation 1,999.20 BCM; utilisable water 1,139 BCM
Precipitation 1,139 BCM; natural runoff after evaporation 690 BCM; utilisable water 4,000 BCM
17.x: India receives about 4,000 BCM of precipitation annually. Natural runoff after evaporation is about 1,999.20 BCM, of which about 1,139 BCM is utilisable.
17.tq: Match the three quantities in their correct sequence and magnitude.
17.sec: Hydrological cycle - processes that belong and those that do not; hydrometeorology  [APPSC]

17.s: The utilisable water resources of India, as stated in the data, comprise
o: 690 BCM of surface water and 449 BCM of groundwater
449 BCM of surface water and 690 BCM of groundwater
690 BCM of groundwater and 1,999.20 BCM of surface water
1,139 BCM of surface water and 690 BCM of groundwater
17.x: The utilisable total of 1,139 BCM consists of approximately 690 BCM of surface water and 449 BCM of groundwater.
17.tq: Split the total into its two stated components.
17.sec: Hydrological cycle - processes that belong and those that do not; hydrometeorology  [APPSC]

17.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Heavy rain bursts may exceed the infiltration capacity of soil.
2. When water pools on the surface, part of it may evaporate instead of recharging aquifers.
3. Concentrated heavy rainfall necessarily increases aquifer recharge.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
17.x: Heavy bursts can exceed soil infiltration capacity. The pooled water may evaporate, thereby reducing rather than necessarily increasing aquifer recharge.
17.tq: Test the cause-and-effect chain rather than assuming that more rain always means more recharge.
17.sec: Hydrological cycle - processes that belong and those that do not; hydrometeorology  [APPSC]

17.s: The sun halo is generally observed as
o: a semicircular arc produced by reflection from raindrops
a ring of about 22° formed by refraction through ice crystals in high cirrostratus clouds
a coloured ring produced by diffraction near the Sun or Moon
a white ring caused by dust particles in the lower atmosphere
17.x: A sun halo is typically a ring of about 22° produced when sunlight is refracted through millions of hexagonal ice crystals in thin, high cirrostratus clouds.
17.tq: Use the distinctive combination of angle, cloud type and ice-crystal mechanism.
17.sec: Optical phenomena - sun halo, rainbow  [APPSC]

17.s:
Consider the following statements about a sun halo:
1. It is associated with thin, high cirrostratus clouds.
2. Its formation involves refraction of sunlight through hexagonal ice crystals.
3. It is typically seen as a ring of approximately 22°.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
17.x: All three statements correctly describe the usual formation and appearance of a sun halo.
17.tq: Recognise the option containing all three linked characteristics of the phenomenon.
17.sec: Optical phenomena - sun halo, rainbow  [APPSC]

17.s: A rainbow is produced primarily by
o: refraction, dispersion and internal reflection of sunlight in raindrops
absorption of sunlight by dust particles followed by scattering
only the external reflection of sunlight from water vapour
diffraction of sunlight by ice crystals in cirrostratus clouds
17.x: A rainbow results from refraction, dispersion and internal reflection of sunlight in raindrops. It is generally observed when the Sun is behind the observer.
17.tq: Distinguish the three-part optical process from the mechanism of a halo or corona.
17.sec: Optical phenomena - sun halo, rainbow  [APPSC]

17.s: For a person observing a rainbow, the Sun is generally positioned
o: below the horizon and in front of the observer
vertically above the raindrops at all times
directly in front of the observer
17.x: A rainbow is seen when sunlight enters raindrops in the direction opposite to the observer; therefore, the Sun is behind the observer.
17.tq: Apply the geometry of the observation rather than recalling only the optical processes.
17.sec: Optical phenomena - sun halo, rainbow  [APPSC]

17.s: A corona around the Sun or Moon is formed mainly by
o: dispersion in raindrops when the Sun is behind the observer
diffraction by small water droplets in thin clouds
refraction through large hexagonal ice crystals
17.x: A corona consists of coloured rings close to the Sun or Moon and is produced by diffraction by small water droplets in thin clouds.
17.tq: Discriminate corona from halo by matching it with diffraction and water droplets.
17.sec: Optical phenomena - sun halo, rainbow  [APPSC]

17.s: Which one of the following statements about the leeward side of a mountain range is correct?
o: Air remains stationary and therefore no precipitation occurs anywhere nearby.
Air descends, cools and becomes saturated throughout the year.
Air ascends, cools and produces the highest rainfall in all cases.
Air descends, warms and becomes drier, producing a rain-shadow area.
17.x: On the leeward side, descending air warms adiabatically and becomes drier, producing a rain-shadow region.
17.tq: Follow the direction of air movement and its effect on temperature and moisture.
17.sec: Rain shadow areas and relief-related precipitation terms  [APPSC]

17.s:
With reference to rainfall in the Western Ghats, consider the following statements:
1. The eastern side receives scanty rainfall as it lies on the leeward side.
2. Peninsular rainfall generally decreases from west to east.
3. The eastern side receives more rainfall than the western side because descending air is moist.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
17.x: The eastern side of the Western Ghats is in the rain shadow and receives scanty rainfall. Peninsular rainfall generally decreases from west to east; descending air is warm and dry, not moist.
17.tq: Test the relief-related reversal between windward and leeward sides.
17.sec: Rain shadow areas and relief-related precipitation terms  [APPSC]

17.s: Which one of the following is correctly associated with the rainfall pattern of Andhra Pradesh?
o: Sileru and Sabari valleys receive less than 51 cm of rainfall.
Rayalaseema lies in a rain-shadow region.
The Eastern Ghats prevent all orographic rainfall in the State.
Hagari Valley records the highest rainfall in the State.
17.x: Rayalaseema lies in a rain-shadow region. Hagari Valley has the lowest rainfall, while Sileru and Sabari valleys receive substantially higher rainfall.
17.tq: Identify the correctly matched regional rainfall characteristic.
17.sec: Rain shadow areas and relief-related precipitation terms  [APPSC]

17.s: The Hagari Valley is notable for having
o: the highest rainfall in Andhra Pradesh, exceeding 150 cm
rainfall confined exclusively to the winter season
the highest snowfall in Andhra Pradesh
the lowest rainfall in Andhra Pradesh, below 51 cm
17.x: Hagari Valley receives the lowest rainfall in Andhra Pradesh, with the annual amount being less than 51 cm.
17.tq: Recall the distinctive extreme value and location together.
17.sec: Rain shadow areas and relief-related precipitation terms  [APPSC]

17.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the Sileru and Sabari valleys?
o: They receive about 140–152 cm of rainfall, aided by the southwest monsoon and orographic effect of the Eastern Ghats.
They are the driest valleys of Andhra Pradesh because they lie on the leeward side of the Eastern Ghats.
They lie in the rain shadow of the Western Ghats and receive less than 51 cm of rainfall.
They receive rainfall only from winter cyclones and have no relief effect.
17.x: The Sileru and Sabari valleys receive about 140–152 cm of rainfall owing to the southwest monsoon and the orographic effect of the Eastern Ghats.
17.tq: Match the higher-rainfall valleys with their range, season and relief mechanism.
17.sec: Rain shadow areas and relief-related precipitation terms  [APPSC]

17.s: Orographic lifting in the Himalayas can produce cloudbursts because it
o: causes all clouds to descend as fog at sea level
forces moist air upward and helps build towering cumulonimbus clouds
prevents vertical development of clouds over the mountains
converts every form of precipitation into snowfall
17.x: Orographic lifting raises moist air over the Himalayas, encouraging the development of towering cumulonimbus clouds capable of producing cloudbursts.
17.tq: Connect relief-induced uplift with vertical cloud development and extreme rainfall.
17.sec: Rain shadow areas and relief-related precipitation terms  [APPSC]

17.s: Dew is formed when
o: smoke mixes with fog in an urban atmosphere
rain freezes while falling through a cold atmospheric layer
moisture condenses on a cool surface and the dew point is above 0°C
water vapour freezes directly into ice crystals below 0°C
17.x: Dew forms when moisture condenses on cool surfaces at a dew point above 0°C. Frost forms as ice crystals when the dew point is at or below 0°C.
17.tq: Separate dew from frost by using the dew-point threshold and physical form.
17.sec: Forms of condensation and precipitation - dew, frost, fog, mist, smog, sleet, hail  [other exams]

17.s: Frost differs from dew because frost
o: is a cloud at ground level with visibility below 1 km
forms only when the dew point is above 0°C
forms as ice crystals when the dew point is at or below 0°C
consists of rain drops larger than 0.5 mm
17.x: Frost forms as ice crystals when the dew point is at or below 0°C. Dew is liquid moisture condensed on cool surfaces with a dew point above 0°C.
17.tq: Use the temperature condition to distinguish two closely related forms of condensation.
17.sec: Forms of condensation and precipitation - dew, frost, fog, mist, smog, sleet, hail  [other exams]

17.s: Which one of the following statements regarding fog and mist is correct?
o: Fog is always drier than mist and forms only during clear afternoons.
Fog is a cloud at ground level with visibility under 1 km, whereas mist generally has visibility over 1 km.
Mist has visibility below 1 km, whereas fog has visibility over 1 km.
Both fog and mist are forms of precipitation falling from cumulonimbus clouds.
17.x: Fog is a cloud at ground level and is associated with visibility under 1 km. Mist is thinner and wetter, with visibility generally over 1 km.
17.tq: Compare the two similar terms through their visibility thresholds.
17.sec: Forms of condensation and precipitation - dew, frost, fog, mist, smog, sleet, hail  [other exams]

17.s: Fog is most likely to form when
o: strong winds remove moisture from the ground rapidly
air remains very warm and dry above its dew point
rain freezes into pellets while falling
air is cooled below its dew point, often under an inversion
17.x: Fog forms when air near the ground is cooled below its dew point. Temperature inversion conditions often favour its formation.
17.tq: Identify the atmospheric condition that causes condensation at ground level.
17.sec: Forms of condensation and precipitation - dew, frost, fog, mist, smog, sleet, hail  [other exams]

17.s:
Which of the following correctly distinguishes London smog from Los Angeles smog?
1. London smog is sulphurous, cool and humid.
2. Los Angeles smog is photochemical and requires sunlight.
3. Photochemical smog can involve the formation of PAN.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
17.x: London smog is sulphurous and associated with cool, humid conditions. Los Angeles smog is photochemical, requires sunlight and can produce PAN.
17.tq: Use the source-condition-product distinction between two types of smog.
17.sec: Forms of condensation and precipitation - dew, frost, fog, mist, smog, sleet, hail  [other exams]

17.s: Sleet is formed when
o: rain freezes into ice pellets while falling through a cold layer
small water droplets diffract sunlight in thin clouds
water vapour condenses directly on a surface above 0°C
ice balls grow in cumulonimbus clouds due to strong updrafts
17.x: Sleet consists of ice pellets formed when rain freezes while passing through a cold atmospheric layer. Hail forms differently within cumulonimbus clouds.
17.tq: Distinguish falling rain that freezes from hail formed inside a thundercloud.
17.sec: Forms of condensation and precipitation - dew, frost, fog, mist, smog, sleet, hail  [other exams]

17.s: Hail is best described as
o: rain that freezes only after reaching the ground
ice crystals deposited directly on exposed surfaces during a calm night
fine liquid drops released from stratus clouds
layered ice balls formed in cumulonimbus clouds with strong updrafts
17.x: Hail consists of layered ice balls developed within cumulonimbus clouds where strong updrafts repeatedly carry water and ice particles upward.
17.tq: Match the precipitation form with its cloud type and formation mechanism.
17.sec: Forms of condensation and precipitation - dew, frost, fog, mist, smog, sleet, hail  [other exams]

17.s: Dew and frost are favoured by which combination of conditions?
o: Clear skies, calm air, high relative humidity and long cold nights
Continuous rainfall, turbulent winds and high atmospheric pressure
High daytime temperature, strong convection and dry air
Cloudy skies, strong winds, low humidity and short nights
17.x: Clear and calm nights allow surfaces to cool efficiently, while high humidity and long cold nights favour dew or frost formation. Clouds and wind tend to prevent them.
17.tq: Select the complete set of conditions favourable to surface condensation.
17.sec: Forms of condensation and precipitation - dew, frost, fog, mist, smog, sleet, hail  [other exams]

17.s: Lambasingi, sometimes called the ‘Kashmir of Andhra Pradesh’, is associated with frost formation at approximately
17.x: Lambasingi is associated with frost conditions at approximately 2°C, illustrating that surface frost may be observed under suitable local conditions near that temperature.
17.tq: Recall the place-linked temperature figure without confusing it with the 0°C threshold.
17.sec: Forms of condensation and precipitation - dew, frost, fog, mist, smog, sleet, hail  [other exams]

17.s: Dust and salt particles in the atmosphere are important because they can act as
o: agents that prevent all cloud formation
layers that stop precipitation from reaching the ground
17.x: Dust and salt particles can attract and hold atmospheric moisture and therefore act as hygroscopic nuclei for condensation.
17.tq: Identify the atmospheric role of suspended particles from their moisture-attracting property.
17.sec: Forms of condensation and precipitation - dew, frost, fog, mist, smog, sleet, hail  [other exams]

17.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Drizzle — drops exceeding 5 mm from cumulonimbus clouds
Sleet — ice crystals deposited directly on surfaces
17.x: Rain consists of drops exceeding 0.5 mm. Drizzle has fine drops under 0.5 mm and commonly comes from stratus clouds; snow consists of ice crystals formed below 0°C.
17.tq: Use the drop-size threshold to separate rain from drizzle and other forms.
17.sec: Forms of condensation and precipitation - dew, frost, fog, mist, smog, sleet, hail  [other exams]

17.s: Drizzle is characterised by
o: fine drops under 0.5 mm, commonly falling from stratus clouds
rain freezing into pellets in a cold layer
large drops exceeding 5 mm from cumulonimbus clouds
layered ice balls formed by strong updrafts
17.x: Drizzle consists of fine drops under 0.5 mm and is commonly associated with stratus clouds.
17.tq: Use the exact size threshold and cloud association to identify the form.
17.sec: Forms of condensation and precipitation - dew, frost, fog, mist, smog, sleet, hail  [other exams]

17.s: Snow is formed when condensation takes place
o: when rain passes through a thin warm layer
above 0°C as liquid droplets on exposed surfaces
17.x: Snow forms as ice crystals when condensation occurs below 0°C.
17.tq: Identify the precipitation form from its temperature condition and physical state.
17.sec: Forms of condensation and precipitation - dew, frost, fog, mist, smog, sleet, hail  [other exams]

17.s: The phenomenon known as ‘blood rain’ may occur when
o: sunlight is refracted through hexagonal ice crystals
raindrops freeze into transparent ice pellets
dust or spores become mixed with raindrops
sulphur dioxide dissolves in snow crystals
17.x: Coloured rain can result when dust or spores mix with raindrops. Sirocco dust over Italy and Kerala’s red rain of 2001 are examples associated with this phenomenon.
17.tq: Match the unusual colour of rain with its suspended material.
17.sec: Forms of condensation and precipitation - dew, frost, fog, mist, smog, sleet, hail  [other exams]

17.s: Kerala’s red rain of 2001 is an example associated with
o: a solar corona caused by water droplets
acid rain caused exclusively by nitrogen oxides
17.x: Kerala’s red rain of 2001 is cited as an example of coloured rain, which may result from dust or spores mixed with rainwater.
17.tq: Link the named event with the correct precipitation category.
17.sec: Forms of condensation and precipitation - dew, frost, fog, mist, smog, sleet, hail  [other exams]

17.s:
Which of the following substances can be used as cloud-seeding agents or condensation nuclei?
1. Silver iodide
2. Potassium iodide
3. Sodium chloride
4. Dry ice
5. Liquid propane
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
17.x: Silver iodide, potassium iodide, sodium chloride, dry ice and liquid propane are all listed as cloud-seeding substances or condensation nuclei.
17.tq: Recognise the complete list rather than excluding less familiar cloud-seeding agents.
17.sec: Forms of condensation and precipitation - dew, frost, fog, mist, smog, sleet, hail  [other exams]

17.s: Cloud seeding is effective only when
o: there is no atmospheric moisture available
the atmosphere is completely cloudless and dry
strong sunlight alone is sufficient, regardless of cloud conditions
suitable moist clouds are already present
17.x: Cloud seeding requires suitable moist clouds; seeding cannot create effective precipitation in the complete absence of appropriate cloud moisture.
17.tq: Test the limiting condition instead of treating cloud seeding as weather creation from nothing.
17.sec: Forms of condensation and precipitation - dew, frost, fog, mist, smog, sleet, hail  [other exams]

17.s: Acid rain is generally defined as precipitation having a pH
17.x: Acid rain is conventionally defined as precipitation with a pH below 5.6, commonly associated with sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides.
17.tq: Recall the standard pH cut-off rather than merely identifying rain as acidic.
17.sec: Forms of condensation and precipitation - dew, frost, fog, mist, smog, sleet, hail  [other exams]

17.s: The term ‘acid rain’ was coined by
17.x: The term ‘acid rain’ was coined by Robert Angus Smith in 1872.
17.tq: Match the environmental term with its originator and year.
17.sec: Forms of condensation and precipitation - dew, frost, fog, mist, smog, sleet, hail  [other exams]

17.s: The principal precursor gases associated with acid rain are
17.x: Acid rain is mainly associated with sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides, which contribute to the formation of acidic compounds in the atmosphere.
17.tq: Identify the pollutant pair most directly linked with the phenomenon.
17.sec: Forms of condensation and precipitation - dew, frost, fog, mist, smog, sleet, hail  [other exams]

17.s: Which combination correctly describes the usual Himalayan setting of cloudbursts given in the data?
o: March to May, above 5,000 m, generally involving stratus clouds
June to August, at elevations of about 1,000–2,500 m, generally involving cumulonimbus clouds
December to February, below 100 m, generally involving cirrostratus clouds
September to November, at sea level, generally involving nimbostratus clouds
17.x: Himalayan cloudbursts commonly occur during June–August at elevations of about 1,000–2,500 m and are associated with cumulonimbus clouds.
17.tq: Combine season, altitude and cloud type to reject partially correct alternatives.
17.sec: Forms of condensation and precipitation - dew, frost, fog, mist, smog, sleet, hail  [other exams]

17.s: Which one of the following correctly defines absolute humidity?
o: The percentage of water vapour present in air relative to its capacity
The temperature at which condensation begins
The mass of water vapour per unit weight of air
The actual water vapour present per unit volume of air
17.x: Absolute humidity is the actual amount of water vapour per unit volume of air, generally expressed in grams per cubic metre (g/m³).
17.tq: Use the exact defining unit to distinguish absolute humidity from specific and relative humidity.
17.sec: Humidity and evaporation - absolute, specific, relative, dew point, saturation, latent heat

17.s:
With reference to humidity, consider the following statements:
1. Specific humidity is expressed as the mass of water vapour per unit weight of air.
2. Specific humidity is unaffected by changes in the volume of air.
3. Relative humidity is expressed as a percentage of the moisture-holding capacity of air at a given temperature.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
17.x: Specific humidity is measured in grams per kilogram of air and is not affected by volume changes. Relative humidity compares actual vapour with the amount air can hold at that temperature.
17.tq: Match each statement with its defining measure and unit before selecting the coded combination.
17.sec: Humidity and evaporation - absolute, specific, relative, dew point, saturation, latent heat

17.s: The temperature at which air becomes saturated and condensation begins is known as:
17.x: The dew point is the temperature at which air becomes saturated and condensation starts.
17.tq: Test the precise distinction between a temperature condition and a humidity measure.
17.sec: Humidity and evaporation - absolute, specific, relative, dew point, saturation, latent heat

17.s: If the actual amount of water vapour in the air remains unchanged and the air temperature rises, what happens to relative humidity?
o: It remains unchanged because the vapour content is constant
It falls because the moisture-holding capacity of air increases
It becomes 100 per cent in all cases
It rises because warm air contains more vapour
17.x: Warm air can hold more water vapour. Therefore, with the same actual vapour content, relative humidity falls as temperature rises and increases on cooling.
17.tq: Apply the same-vapour rule rather than confusing moisture content with relative humidity.
17.sec: Humidity and evaporation - absolute, specific, relative, dew point, saturation, latent heat

17.s: Relative humidity reaches saturation when it is:
17.x: Saturation occurs when relative humidity is 100 per cent, meaning that the air contains the maximum moisture it can hold at that temperature.
17.tq: Use the threshold value directly for a quantitative definition question.
17.sec: Humidity and evaporation - absolute, specific, relative, dew point, saturation, latent heat

17.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Latent heat is absorbed during evaporation.
2. Latent heat is released during condensation.
3. The release of latent heat contributes to the energy of thunderstorms and cyclones.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
17.x: Evaporation absorbs latent heat, while condensation releases it. This released energy helps power thunderstorms and cyclones.

17.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the broad distribution of atmospheric water vapour?
o: It remains uniform at about 4 per cent from the equator to the poles
It is up to about 4 per cent in humid tropical areas and under 1 per cent in deserts and polar areas
It is under 1 per cent in the humid tropics and above 4 per cent in deserts
It is highest in deserts and polar areas and decreases in the humid tropics

17.s: Which of the following statements regarding atmospheric moisture is correct?
o: Water vapour generally increases with altitude because of falling pressure
Relative humidity is always lower over oceans than over continents
Relative humidity is generally higher over oceans than over continents, and water vapour falls with altitude
Warm air holds less water vapour than cold air

Specific humidity — grams of vapour per kilogram of air
Relative humidity — grams of vapour per cubic metre of air

Coastal Andhra generally records below 30 per cent relative humidity throughout the year

18.s: Which one of the following best defines an air mass?

A very large body of air having nearly uniform temperature and humidity horizontally
A vertical layer of air with uniform pressure but varying humidity

o: cT — Sahara and Arabia — hot and dry
mE — Equatorial oceans — hot and very humid

mP — High-latitude oceans — cool and moist
18.x: cA originates over the Arctic basin and Greenland ice, not tropical oceans. It is very cold and very dry.

18.s: The Siberian High, Canadian High and Antarctic High are examples of:
18.x: Cold, dense cP and cA air masses build polar anticyclones, which are cold-core highs and strongest near the surface.

18.s: Which combination of weather conditions is associated with cold-core polar anticyclones?
o: Clear skies, fog, frost and sharp night cooling
Continuous convection, cumulonimbus and torrential rain
Warm nights, high humidity and prolonged drizzle
Persistent humid heat and widespread nimbostratus

18.s: An air mass is modified after leaving its source region mainly because it:

Is heated or cooled from below and gains or loses moisture
Changes its Bergeron code immediately through vertical ascent
Can move only along a stationary front

18.s: When cold air moves over a warmer surface, which one of the following conditions develops?
o: The air loses all moisture and produces frost
The air is heated from below and becomes unstable
The air is cooled from below and becomes stable
The air becomes stable and produces only drizzle
18.x: Cold air moving over a warmer surface is heated from below, becomes unstable and promotes convection, cumulus clouds and showers.

18.s: Warm air moving over a colder surface generally produces:
o: Cumulus, squalls and sudden temperature fall
Clear skies and sharp night cooling only

18.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Dust and salt particles can act as hygroscopic nuclei for condensation.

3. Water vapour has no role in controlling atmospheric stability.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
18.x: Dust and salt act as hygroscopic condensation nuclei, and water vapour may reach up to 4 percent by volume in the humid tropics. Water vapour does influence atmospheric stability, so statement 3 is false.

Formation of cP air over Arabia

o: Sloping boundary zone between air masses of different temperature and density
Boundary between land and ocean heat regimes
Vertical centre of a high-pressure cell

18.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
o: Cold front — gentle slope — prolonged light rain ahead
Warm front — steep slope — sudden heavy showers
Stationary front — neither air mass advances — rain may persist for days
Occluded front — warm air remains at the ground — no mixed weather
18.x: At a stationary front neither air mass advances, and cloud and rain may persist for days. Cold fronts are steep, warm fronts have gentle slopes, and occlusion lifts warm air off the ground.
18.tq: Match the front type with its defining movement rather than only its cloud type.

18.s: A cold front is characterised by which one of the following combinations?
o: Warm air riding gradually over retreating cold air and prolonged light rain
Cold air advancing and lifting warm air sharply, with heavy short showers and a sudden temperature fall
A faster warm front overtaking a cold front
Neither air mass advancing and rainfall persisting for several days
18.x: In a cold front, advancing cold air forms a steep wedge and lifts warm air sharply, producing cumulonimbus, heavy short showers, thunder, squalls and a sudden temperature fall.
18.tq: Use the movement of the advancing air mass as the key discriminator.
18.sec: Fronts - cold, warm, stationary, occluded

18.s: In a warm front, warm air:
o: Sinks beneath advancing cold air along a steep slope
Overtakes the cold front and produces occlusion immediately
Remains trapped between two stationary air masses
Rides up over retreating cold air along a gentle slope
18.x: A warm front has a gentle slope because warm air rides up over retreating cold air, producing a wide belt of layered cloud and prolonged light-to-moderate rain ahead of the front.

18.s: The occluded front represents the stage when:
o: A warm front overtakes a cold front and pushes cold air upward
Two warm air masses converge over an ocean
A faster cold front overtakes a warm front and lifts warm air off the ground
A stationary front begins to weaken without movement
18.x: An occluded front forms when a faster cold front overtakes a warm front, lifting the warm air from the ground. It is the last stage of a temperate cyclone.

At the leading edge of thunderstorm outflows or cold fronts
At the top of the stratosphere
Only at the centre of an anticyclone

Warm humid conditions and no cloud
Only prolonged light rain without temperature change

o: Dissolution of a front as temperature contrast disappears
Formation or sharpening of a front due to convergence of contrasting air masses
Movement of a warm front over a stationary ocean
Complete absence of temperature contrast between air masses

Frontolysis is weakening and dissolution as temperature contrast is lost, whereas frontogenesis forms or sharpens a front

19.s: The strongest winds and heaviest rainfall in a tropical cyclone are generally found in the:

19.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the rain bands of a tropical cyclone?

A ring of sinking air at the centre
Spiral bands of cloud and rain outside the eyewall
Concentric bands of clear air inside the eye

19.tq: Test the location-function match within cyclone structure.

19.s: How wide is the eye of a tropical cyclone generally described as being?

19.s: In which direction do tropical cyclones rotate in the Northern and Southern Hemispheres respectively?

19.s: Which statement correctly explains the usual movement of tropical cyclones over the oceans?
o: They remain stationary because steering winds are absent.
Westerlies move every tropical cyclone directly towards the equator.
Trade winds push them eastward, while westerlies always move them towards the south-west.
Trade winds generally push them westward, while westerlies may recurve mature storms towards the north-east.
19.x: Trade winds steer tropical cyclones westward towards eastern continental coasts. In mature systems, westerlies may recurve them towards the north-east.
19.tq: Follow the steering-wind sequence from initial westward movement to later recurvature.

19.s: A tropical cyclone weakens after landfall primarily because it:
o: Receives excessive moisture from the land surface
Enters a region of stronger Coriolis force
Is cut off from its warm, moist oceanic energy source

19.tq: Identify the causal link between landfall and loss of the oceanic energy source.

19.s: Marine heatwaves can increase the wind speed of tropical cyclones by up to approximately:

19.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes a tornado from a hurricane?

A tornado is hundreds of kilometres wide and forms only over warm oceans.
A hurricane is a land-based funnel lasting only a few minutes.
Both phenomena have the same size, duration and place of origin.

Movement exclusively from east to west

They remain stationary over their place of origin
From east to west under the influence of the trade winds
From north to south under the influence of polar easterlies alone

19.s: Which of the following comparisons between tropical and temperate cyclones is correct?
o: Tropical cyclones move west to east, whereas temperate cyclones move east to west.
Tropical cyclones have clear fronts, whereas temperate cyclones have none.
Tropical cyclones originate over land and sea, whereas temperate cyclones originate only over warm seas.
Tropical cyclones are smaller and more intense, whereas temperate cyclones are larger and generally gentler.

Mango showers — snowfall in the Himalayan region
